meta.title: Division 296 and the prudential framework
meta.subtitle: What Australia's new tax on large superannuation balances asks of prudential regulation — and what it does not
meta.basis: Prepared from publicly available sources. Not an official publication of any regulator, and not affiliated with APRA, the ATO or Treasury. Claims marked [S] sourced · [I] inferred · [C] created — see Annex C.

bottom_line.text: This is not a proposal. Division 296 received Royal Assent on 13 March 2026 and commenced on 1 April 2026. It first applies from the 2026-27 income year, so the first measurement year has been running since 1 July 2026. The final regulations were registered on 18 June 2026, thirteen days before that year began, and the ATO's law companion ruling explaining how to perform the calculation has not yet been published.

It is unlikely to be a liquidity event, though that comparison is this note's, not an official one. APRA's System Risk Stress Test had six large funds absorb $174 billion of cumulative demand — just under 16 per cent of net assets, peaking near $30 billion a month — while largely avoiding unlisted sales, selling listed equities instead. No official estimate of Division 296 outflow exists; scaling Treasury's superseded-design costing to the APRA-regulated share gives an indicative $0.9 billion a year, of the order of 1 per cent of the lump sums those funds already pay. On that order of magnitude a forced-asset-sale framing is not supported. The residual risk is composition, not cash: meeting calls by selling listed assets lifted the unlisted share of MySuper options from roughly 29 to 37 per cent.

The material change is that a trustee judgement now feeds an individual member's personal tax bill. Any APRA-regulated fund with more than six members and at least one member above the threshold must split fund earnings on a 'fair and reasonable' basis it designs itself, and produce that figure to the ATO on request — 28 calendar days for most funds, 10 business days for defined benefit interests. Two funds holding identical assets for identical members can lawfully report different numbers; how far apart has never been measured, and that dispersion is the most consequential unknown here. None of the 27 instruments examined governs how the judgement is made, signed off or checked.

The prudential framework mostly already covers this. Of 27 instruments examined, 11 need no change, 11 need supervisory attention, 4 warrant updated guidance, and exactly one needs amending — SRS 611.0, APRA's own member accounts collection, whose top bracket is an open-ended '$1,000,000+', so it cannot tell a $1.1 million account from a $20 million one. The gaps are guidance, supervisory attention and data — not authority.

all_headline_numbers.figure: $3 million and $10 million thresholds; additional 15% above the first and a further 10% above the second; both indexed to CPI; applies from 1 July 2026
all_headline_numbers.meaning: The enacted design. An affected person pays extra tax only on the share of earnings attributable to the balance above the threshold, so someone just over $3 million pays very little and the amount rises steeply with balance. Both thresholds move with inflation, so the 2023 criticism about unindexed thresholds no longer applies.
all_headline_numbers.source: ATO, 'Better targeted superannuation concessions', new legislation guidance (thresholds described as LSBT $3m and VLSBT $10m for 2026-27, 'indexed in line with CPI')

all_headline_numbers.meaning: The top reporting bracket is one third of the lower Division 296 threshold and one tenth of the upper. APRA cannot count, locate or size the affected population from its own collections. Because the collection is keyed to the member account within a single fund, while the tax threshold is measured across all of a person's superannuation, more brackets would improve visibility of large accounts but still could not produce the threshold view - only the ATO holds that.
all_headline_numbers.source: Reporting Standard SRS 611.0 Member Accounts, SRF 611.0 Instructions, Members Benefit Bracket Type valid values (Table 1 Column 3; Table 2 Column 4) - verified against the instrument text

all_headline_numbers.figure: 23 RSE licensees reviewed, holding $2,018 billion at 30 June 2024 (around 80% of APRA-regulated superannuation assets) and 18.7 million member accounts; 12 of the 23 require material improvement
all_headline_numbers.meaning: CORRECTED from the draft, which attached the $2,018bn and 18.7m figures to the 12 licensees rather than to the full review population - roughly doubling the apparent scale of the adverse finding. The accurate statement is that the scope figures describe all 23; 12 of them require material improvement in valuation governance, liquidity risk management or both (8 on each limb).
all_headline_numbers.source: APRA, 'Governance of unlisted asset valuation and liquidity risk management in superannuation', 17 December 2024

all_headline_numbers.figure: The liquidity subgroup requiring material improvement represents 27% of funds under management and 5.4 million member accounts
all_headline_numbers.meaning: The correctly sized adverse finding, as distinct from the review's total scope. This is the figure to use when describing how much of the system sits with licensees APRA has already judged to need material improvement on liquidity risk management.
all_headline_numbers.source: APRA, 'Governance of unlisted asset valuation and liquidity risk management in superannuation', 17 December 2024

all_headline_numbers.figure: 11 of 23 licensees had a dedicated valuation committee; committee members 'included individuals whose remuneration may be dependent on the outcome of the valuation process'; 'Some assets may not be revalued for multiple quarters at a time'
all_headline_numbers.meaning: APRA has already published adverse findings on the precise control that now also influences a member's personal tax position, because the 30 June balance determines both whether a member is over the threshold and the proportion of earnings taxed. The more likely complaint direction is upward revaluation lifting members over the threshold, which happens innocently, rather than downward suppression, which would require alleging misconduct.
all_headline_numbers.source: APRA, 'Governance of unlisted asset valuation and liquidity risk management in superannuation', 17 December 2024 (quotes verified verbatim)

all_headline_numbers.figure: Stress test: $174 billion cumulative liquidity demand (just under 16% of net assets), peak monthly calls around $30 billion (less than 7% of available liquid assets); funds sold $81 billion of equities and $11 billion of fixed income and 'largely avoided selling unlisted assets to meet liquidity needs'
all_headline_numbers.meaning: RESTATED - the draft's claim that funds met the shock 'without selling a single unlisted asset' is not what the report says and should not be repeated. The accurate version still makes the point: under a severe shock, funds met very large calls primarily by selling listed assets and largely avoided unlisted sales. This is the right calibration against which to judge Division 296 outflow, which is far smaller.
all_headline_numbers.source: APRA, System Risk Stress Test, 30 June 2026 (quotes verified verbatim)

all_headline_numbers.figure: Allocations to illiquid assets in MySuper options increased substantially under the stress test, with the unlisted share rising from roughly 29% to 37%
all_headline_numbers.meaning: Because funds met the shock by selling listed assets, the unlisted share of the remaining portfolio rose sharply. This is the composition effect to watch rather than a cash shortfall, and it is the reason liquidity should not be dismissed entirely even though aggregate Division 296 outflow is small.
all_headline_numbers.source: APRA, System Risk Stress Test, 30 June 2026

all_headline_numbers.figure: ATO information requests: defined benefit and certain other interests from November 2027 with 10 business days to respond; other APRA-regulated funds from April with 28 calendar days; early assessments from March 2028
all_headline_numbers.meaning: TIMING DISCREPANCY DISCLOSED. The indicative date for non-defined-benefit APRA funds moved between meetings: the 18 February 2026 record refers to 'APRA RFIs February 2028' (timed to follow income tax returns due end of January 2028), while the 20 May 2026 record refers to requests commencing in April. These are ATO indicative planning dates, not settled deadlines; the ATO has said requests may issue outside these timeframes and that it will consider extensions in the first year. The 10 business day window for defined benefit funds is consistent across both records.
all_headline_numbers.source: ATO Superannuation Administration Group key messages, 18 February 2026 and 20 May 2026 (cited separately because they differ)

all_headline_numbers.figure: Income Tax Assessment (1997 Act) Amendment (Building a Stronger and Fairer Super System and Other Measures) Regulations 2026 (F2026L00726) registered 18 June 2026
all_headline_numbers.meaning: The regulations were registered thirteen days before the first measurement year began on 1 July 2026. Every dividend, rent payment and asset sale since that date is already inside the tax base, while the ATO's detailed guidance on how to perform the calculation and attribution is still being developed through its co-design process.
all_headline_numbers.source: Federal Register of Legislation, F2026L00726 (title and registration date verified)

all_headline_numbers.figure: Payday Super also first applies from 1 July 2026 (the start of the 2026-27 income year), requiring contributions to be allocated or returned within three business days; APRA wrote to all RSE licensees on 25 March 2026 warning that a material number were not on track to deliver SuperStream 3.0
all_headline_numbers.meaning: Two major changes landed on the same administration systems on the same day, competing for the same finite administrator change capacity - and Payday Super carried the earlier, more visible deadline. This is the change-saturation risk. It also supplies a precedent: the Payday Super letter did exactly what is proposed here for Division 296, including stating that contribution processing should be treated as a CPS 230 critical operation and that significant breaches 'would necessitate a breach notification to APRA' under s29JA of the SIS Act.
all_headline_numbers.source: APRA, 'Payday Super Readiness' letter to all RSE licensees, 25 March 2026

all_headline_numbers.figure: CPS 230 para 50 requires RSE licensees to classify providers of 'fund administration, custodial services, investment management and arrangements with promoters and financial planners' as material service providers; para 51 requires the register to be submitted to APRA annually
all_headline_numbers.meaning: APRA already receives, annually, the dataset that maps which licensees depend on which administrators and custodians. Because the Division 296 calculation, attribution, reporting and payment will be delivered largely by a small number of shared providers, this existing collection can be used to identify how many licensees share a single build - and therefore where a defect would be a common-mode failure across many funds at once. No new collection is required. APRA published a register template on 17 October 2024, with superannuation trustees required to submit by 1 October 2025.
all_headline_numbers.source: Prudential Standard CPS 230 (July 2025 version), paras 50 and 51, verified verbatim; APRA, 'APRA releases material service provider register template', 17 October 2024

why_prudential.text: The tax is assessed on the member, but the work lands on the trustee — a calculation and attribution function that did not exist before, and that no prudential standard was written for.

The attribution standard is a discretion, not a formula. The dividing line is member count, not which regulator applies: funds with more than six members design their own 'fair and reasonable' basis, while funds of six or fewer — including APRA's own small funds — get a prescribed formula and an annual actuarial certificate. The principles-based test therefore falls on every APRA-regulated fund of any size.

It is a member-equity problem wearing a tax label. A whole-of-fund tax figure and a daily unit price cannot be reconciled exactly, so any method advantages some members over others — and ASFA has asked that the judgement sit outside AFCA's reach.

There is a hard new duty on a short clock: 14 days for a fund to tell the ATO when an end benefit will be paid, and 7 to correct a material error. The Commissioner keeps the Division 296 debt account for decades, so the fund's member-level records behind it must survive mergers, transfers and changes of administrator — on a transfer protocol that has not yet been settled.

The affected population is largely invisible to the prudential regulator. APRA's highest published balance bracket is $1 million, and more brackets would show where the very large accounts sit — but because the threshold spans everything a person holds across every fund, no per-fund collection can produce the threshold view. Only the ATO holds that.

provisions_intro: A note on where to look, because the numbering misleads. Division 296 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 does not itself place obligations on funds — its own Guide points to the Taxation Administration Act for the administration rules, and the term 'RSE licensee' does not appear in the Act at all. It uses 'superannuation provider'. The table below sets out where each part of the machinery actually sits.

provisions.heading: Object of this Division
provisions.what: A single objects clause, s 296-5, and nothing else. It imposes no obligation on the trustee, the member or the Commissioner. Its only legal work is interpretive — but that matters here, because it is the lens against which a trustee's 'fair and reasonable' attribution would be construed.

provisions.heading: Better targeted superannuation concessions
provisions.what: Where the tax actually bites: liability (s 296-15), both thresholds (ss 296-30, 296-35), taxable and total superannuation earnings, Division 296 fund earnings (s 296-60), and the separate treatment of defined benefit and other interests (s 296-70).

provisions.heading: Division 296 end benefit notice
provisions.what: The clearest new duty on a fund. Where the Commissioner keeps a Division 296 debt account for an interest and the end benefit becomes payable, the provider must notify the Commissioner of the expected payment date within 14 days, in the approved form. The section carries an express note that a dissatisfied person may complain under the AFCA scheme.

provisions.heading: Material changes or omissions
provisions.what: A material change or omission in a s 134-140 notice must be corrected within 7 days of the fund becoming aware of it.

provisions.heading: Release authorities
provisions.what: Extends the existing release authority machinery to Division 296, so a member can direct that the liability be paid from their superannuation.

provisions.heading: Attribution method
provisions.what: The 'fair and reasonable' attribution standard for funds with more than six members, and the prescribed formula plus actuarial certificate for funds with six or fewer. Made 11 June 2026, registered 18 June 2026 — thirteen days before the first measurement year began.

perimeter.title: Most of the affected population sits outside the prudential perimeter
perimeter.subtitle: Treasury expected 31,800 of about 80,000 affected individuals to sit in APRA-regulated funds or exempt public sector schemes

framework_intro: The most useful finding here is a negative one. Division 296 does not require the prudential framework to be rewritten. Of 27 instruments examined: 11 need no change at all, 11 need only supervisory attention, 4 warrant updated guidance, and exactly one needs amending — SRS 611.0, APRA's own member accounts collection, whose top bracket opens at $1,000,000 — a third of the lower threshold — and is not subdivided above it. The authority already exists. SPS 530 requires a Board-approved investment stress testing programme covering adverse scenarios, and SPG 530 para 79(e) expressly names a change in government policy affecting access to accrued member assets as a liquidity stress factor a prudent licensee would consider; CPS 230 para 36(c) requires an RSE licensee to classify investment management and fund administration as critical operations unless it can justify otherwise. What is missing is guidance confirming these obligations apply to a tax event as much as a market one, supervisory attention on the cohort facing the hardest attribution problem, and data granular enough to observe how the measure lands.

recommendations.text: The attribution work still under way is the last point at which prudential and member-outcomes considerations can be reflected in how the measure operates. The attribution rule itself is settled in the final regulations; what remains open is the ATO's guidance on applying it, developed with industry through a co-design process. APRA engages with Treasury and the ATO.

Confirming that existing obligations already attach would not require a new instrument: fund administration as a critical operation under CPS 230 para 36(c), investment stress testing covering adverse scenarios under SPS 530, and the annual risk management declaration under SPS 220. SPG 530 already names policy-driven liquidity stress as a factor a prudent licensee would consider, but it is guidance rather than an enforceable standard.
The material service provider registers APRA already holds can map which administrators will build this for how many funds, allowing engagement provider by provider rather than licensee by licensee.

A defensible cohort can be built from material APRA already holds: platform, wrap and member-directed trustees, where members choose their own investments so the attribution method changes the answer, and which show the highest concentration of accounts above $1 million in APRA's Quarterly Superannuation Fund Statistics (March 2026, Table 3). The December 2024 thematic is indicative of governance capacity in that group, not evidence about tax administration.

Modelling the 30 June 2027 measurement date falls within the investment stress testing programme SPS 530 already requires, and SPG 530 para 79(e) gives policy-driven events as an example of a liquidity stress factor a prudent licensee would consider.

Two parts of the data gap sit within APRA's own collections: the SRS 611.0 balance brackets could be extended above the thresholds, and outflows decomposed by driver. The third does not — an ATO information-sharing route for total superannuation balance turns on whether the taxation secrecy provisions permit it. If they do not, the remedy is legislative and belongs to Treasury.

redteam_intro: The draft register was attacked by three independent adversarial reviewers before it reached this page: a hostile fact-checker instructed to refute rather than agree, a grading sceptic instructed to hunt for inflated ratings, and a completeness critic instructed to find what had been left out. Every challenge was dispositioned — accepted and fixed, partially accepted, or rejected with reasons. The table below is the full record, including the challenges rejected.

issues.title: One administrator's calculation engine will serve many funds at once, and APRA already holds the register that maps it
issues.plain_english: About fifty licensed super trustees must now work out, for each member with a very large balance, how much of the fund's investment income belongs to that member, report it to the Tax Office, and pay money out when the Tax Office demands it. They will not build fifty separate systems to do this. A small number of shared administration providers, custodians and external tax agents will build it once and run it for many funds. That is efficient, but it means one flawed build, or one provider that is late, is not one fund's problem - it is the same problem in every client fund, in the same few weeks, in the first year. It also means dozens of boards will in practice adopt a supplier's judgement about how to split income between members and call it their own. APRA does not need new data to see this: it already required every trustee to lodge a register of its material service providers by 1 October 2025, for exactly the purpose of spotting concentrations like this one.
issues.why_it_matters: This is the single largest operational-resilience feature of the measure and it is the one that turns an ordinary implementation risk into a correlated, industry-wide one. It also cuts against the assumption that a board-approved methodology means an independently formed methodology. The offsetting point is genuinely positive for a CEO conversation: APRA is not blind here. It holds the dataset that maps which licensees share which administrator, so it can size this exposure at essentially zero collection cost and target engagement at the providers rather than one licensee at a time.

issues.recommended_apra_position: Use the material service provider registers already held to map, before the December 2026 quarter, which administrators, custodians and tax agents will deliver the Division 296 calculation, attribution, lodgement and release-authority function, and how many licensees sit behind each. Then engage provider by provider rather than licensee by licensee. Ask exposed licensees three questions: (a) is the Division 296 function inside the material service provider arrangement, with defined service levels tied to the Tax Office's response windows; (b) where the provider supplies the attribution method, what independent review did the board obtain before adopting it as its own; (c) what happens if the provider cannot deliver by the measurement date, and is that scenario in the tolerance levels and business continuity testing. Consider stating in guidance that the trustee's accountability for a 'fair and reasonable' attribution is non-delegable even where the calculation is performed by a supplier.
issues.who_bears_it: Every RSE licensee sharing a common administrator; concentrated first in platform, wrap and mid-sized licensees that outsource most of the administration stack. Members bear it through simultaneous mis-reporting across multiple funds.
evidence_refs: GRADING RULE APPLIED TO THIS REGISTER (state on the page): Grade A where apra_proximity >= 4 AND materiality >= 4 AND likelihood >= 3. Grade B where the A test fails but materiality + likelihood + apra_proximity >= 9. Grade C where the sum is 8 or less. Applied mechanically; no overrides used. Likelihood throughout is scored as the probability that the named ADVERSE CONSEQUENCE crystallises in the named window, not the probability that a present-tense fact is true.

INFERRED CHAIN: (1) the Division 296 calculation, attribution, Tax Office lodgement and release-authority payment are all fund administration functions; (2) fund administration is overwhelmingly outsourced to a small number of providers, and the fund income tax return from which fund earnings derive is often prepared by an external tax agent; (3) therefore a single methodology or build defect propagates simultaneously across every client fund; (4) the CPS 230 service provider limb, not only the critical operations limb, is the governing requirement; (5) APRA already holds the register that identifies the providers.
GAP: the register does not yet identify WHICH providers dominate the Division 296 build. That is an internal data query, not new collection, and should be run before the meeting.

issues.title: Fund administration must now perform a new statutory calculation, reporting and payment function on someone else's clock
issues.plain_english: From 1 July 2026 every dividend, rent payment and asset sale is already inside the tax base for the first measurement year. Three new jobs now sit in fund administration and none of them existed before. First, work out the fund's taxable earnings and split them across affected members, then answer the Tax Office when it asks - defined benefit and alternative-method funds are indicated to get ten business days, other funds twenty-eight calendar days. Second, when the Tax Office sends a release notice, pay the money out of the member's super on a short clock, with a penalty for missing it. Third, when the fund later amends its tax return - which happens routinely, because income from unlisted and overseas investments is often not final when the return is due - the change flows back through to members' personal tax assessments, for up to four years. The Tax Office guidance explaining how to do the calculation has not been published.
issues.why_it_matters: This is one exposure, not three, and it is the exposure the whole measure comes down to for an APRA-regulated fund: a new statutory calculation and payment function, largely outsourced, performed to external deadlines that all fall in the same annual window across the industry. The consequence of failure leaves the fund and lands on an identified member's personal tax position. The first external test is roughly sixteen to twenty months away, and by the time it fails the underlying FY2026-27 data is historical and cannot be reconstructed.

issues.recommended_apra_position: Treat Division 296 readiness as compliance with operative law, not contingency planning, and test it with document-based questions in FY2027 engagements: has the licensee set CPS 230 tolerance levels for the Division 296 calculation, reporting and release-authority processes inside fund administration; are Division 296 failure scenarios in business continuity testing; does the FY2027 risk appetite statement and risk management declaration address it; has the FY2027 Operational Risk Financial Requirement target amount moved. Gate the expectation on exposure - for a licensee with a handful of in-scope members, not moving the target amount is a proportionate judgement, not a governance failure. Set expectations for adaptable rather than hard-coded builds while the Tax Office guidance is unsettled; day-one perfection is not the standard. Also treat the Division 296 dataset - which identifies by name the members with the largest balances in the country, assembled and transmitted largely by outsourced administrators - as a new information asset that should be classified in the CPS 234 information asset register.
issues.who_bears_it: All RSE licensees with in-scope members; first and hardest on defined benefit and alternative-method funds, which face the shorter response window. Members bear mis-calculation through their personal tax assessments; legal personal representatives and estates bear the amendment cascade.

issues.title: A trustee judgement now drives an identified member's personal tax bill, and no instrument governs how that judgement is made
issues.plain_english: A fund with more than six members must split its investment income across affected members on a 'fair and reasonable' basis. The law does not say how. Two funds holding identical investments for identical members can lawfully report different numbers. To be precise about what that number does: it is an input the Tax Office uses to assess the member, not the member's tax bill itself. The Tax Office assesses the individual, and the individual can object to that assessment. But the trustee's number is what the assessment is built on. Here is what is at stake, which no version of this note has stated: only the slice of earnings above three million dollars is taxed. A member with $3.2 million earning six per cent owes roughly $1,800. At $4 million, roughly $9,000. At $10 million, roughly $63,000. So for members just over the line, differences between lawful methods are worth tens of dollars; for members well above it, and particularly in options where members pick their own investments, they can be worth real money. Nobody has set a standard for how a fund makes the judgement, how a board signs it off, or who independently checks it.
issues.why_it_matters: This is a new, recurring exercise of trustee power over identified members, with no prescribed method, no external assurance and no APRA line of sight. It engages the covenants to act in members' best financial interests and to treat members fairly as between members. Because the first measurement year is already running, a methodology not documented now cannot be reconstructed when the Tax Office ruling lands - which is the classic precondition for a remediation programme in FY2029. The honest qualification is that nobody has measured how far two lawful methods actually diverge, so the size of the equity problem is currently asserted rather than known.

issues.title: Three separate blind spots on the same process: no auditor assurance, no APRA reporting standard, and no breach-notification trigger
issues.plain_english: The largest new calculation these funds will ever perform sits outside all three of APRA's normal ways of finding out something has gone wrong. The fund auditor's assurance covers data reported under APRA's reporting standards and compliance with superannuation law; this calculation is reported to the Tax Office under tax law, so it falls outside both. There is no APRA reporting form that collects anything about it. And the duty to tell APRA about a significant breach is tied to breaches of superannuation licensing law, which this is not - so a late, incomplete or materially wrong report to the Tax Office is not by itself something the fund must tell APRA about. It becomes reportable only indirectly, if it shows the fund's compliance arrangements are inadequate or a member loses money. The practical result is that APRA is likely to hear about a systemic failure late, or from the Tax Office.
issues.why_it_matters: An assurance gap on a high-consequence, member-specific calculation is the pattern that precedes a large remediation. Three independent blind spots layered on the same process is worse than any one of them. The fix is the cheapest recommendation available in this pack: APRA can state its notification expectation in a letter, with no instrument change and without waiting for a reporting standard amendment that cannot deliver in time. APRA did exactly this for another measure commencing the same day.

issues.title: Removing the tax on paper gains did not close the valuation file - the 30 June unit price still decides who is caught and how much
issues.plain_english: The earlier 2023 version of this tax would have taxed increases in the value of assets that had not been sold. That is gone, and any argument built on forced sales to pay tax on paper gains is obsolete. But valuation still matters twice over: a member's balance at 30 June decides whether they are over the threshold at all, and the same balance sets what share of the fund's earnings is taxed. That balance comes from the unit price, which comes from how the fund values assets that are not traded on a market. The direction most people assume - that funds might hold valuations down to keep wealthy members under the line - is the less likely one, because it requires misconduct and it damages every other member's exit price. The more likely and more awkward direction is upward: a routine revaluation at 30 June pushes members over the line or raises their taxed share, entirely innocently, and the fund has to answer the complaint. APRA has already published findings that only eleven of twenty-three large trustees had a dedicated valuation committee, that some committees included people whose pay may depend on the valuation outcome, and that some assets go unvalued for several quarters.
issues.why_it_matters: The conflict is smaller than under the old design but sharper in character: it now touches a small, wealthy, individually identifiable group and produces a personal tax consequence, not only a unit-pricing one. The reputational exposure runs to APRA as much as to trustees, because APRA published adverse findings on this exact control in December 2024 and knew the measure first applies from 1 July 2026 (the start of the 2026-27 income year). Supervisors should not treat the removal of unrealised-gains taxation as closing the valuation governance question.

issues.title: APRA cannot see the affected population, and the obvious remedy - Tax Office data - may not be lawful without amendment
issues.plain_english: The tax applies above three million dollars and again above ten million. The highest balance band APRA collects and publishes is 'one million and above'. So APRA cannot count members above three million, cannot see where they are concentrated, and cannot size a fund's exposure. A deeper problem sits behind that: the threshold is measured across everything a person holds, in every fund including a self-managed one. APRA's collections are per fund and per account, so more balance bands would still not produce that view. Only the Tax Office holds it. But the obvious fix - a standing data feed from the Tax Office - runs into taxpayer secrecy law, and nobody has checked whether it is permitted. There is also a quieter gap: APRA collects nothing at all about the Division 296 process itself - not how many in-scope members a fund reports, not which method it uses, not how many release notices it received. Balance bands tell APRA who is exposed; a single process question would tell APRA who is ready.
issues.why_it_matters: Without this, every APRA statement about the measure's effect on regulated funds is an estimate rather than an observation, and APRA cannot challenge a licensee that says it has very few affected members. It is also the main reputational risk in a CEO-level conversation: APRA should not promise to monitor a population it structurally cannot see. The honest framing is that APRA can monitor large-account behaviour in APRA-regulated funds, not the affected population.

issues.title: A new statutory duty attaches to a debt account that must survive mergers, transfers and administrator changes for decades
issues.plain_english: For members whose tax is deferred - principally defined benefit members - the Tax Office keeps a running debt account and collects when the benefit is finally paid. That creates a new, concrete duty on the fund: when the end benefit becomes payable, it must tell the Tax Office the expected payment date within fourteen days, in the approved form, and correct any material change or omission within seven days. This is the clearest new obligation the law places on a fund, and it is not a one-off. The record that triggers it may have to survive thirty or forty years, a fund merger, a transfer to another fund and two or three changes of administrator. The provision carries an express note that a person who is dissatisfied may complain through the external complaints scheme - which cuts against the industry request that Division 296 trustee judgements sit outside that scheme.
issues.why_it_matters: This is a long-duration data custody obligation with a short-fuse notification duty on the end of it, and it is the point where the register's operational and record-keeping themes meet the sector's consolidation agenda. APRA actively encourages fund mergers; an unresolved transfer protocol for debt account and Division 296 data puts two APRA objectives in tension. The express complaints note is also useful ammunition: it indicates Parliament contemplated member recourse against the provider, which is directly relevant to how APRA reads the industry's carve-out request.

issues.title: Defined benefit funds must build an annual actuarial valuation capability they have never had, from a very small pool of providers
issues.plain_english: For a defined benefit member there is no pot of money to look at, so an actuary has to estimate what the promised pension is worth. The tax looks at how much that estimate rose over the year, cut by about seventeen and a half per cent. Funds have only ever done this estimate one member at a time, by hand, when a couple divorced. Now they must do it for every member, every year, and they face the shorter response window when the Tax Office asks. A small number of consulting actuarial firms will do this for essentially every defined benefit scheme in the country, on the same timetable - a concentration in its own right. For small corporate schemes with a handful of members, the annual cost may simply not be economic, which is a plausible trigger for winding up. One thing to be clear about: defined benefit members are measured on the movement in value, not on income actually received, so they are on a different basis from everyone else. That is Parliament's choice, not the trustee's, and a trustee does not breach its duty of fairness by applying the law - but it will have to explain it.
issues.why_it_matters: This is a genuinely new operational and actuarial capability, concentrated in about ten public sector licensees plus a small number of corporate schemes, delivered by a handful of external providers on a tight clock. It is an operational and viability question, not an equity failing. There is no near-term call on fund solvency, because the tax on a defined benefit interest is deferred to a debt account, so SPS 160's shortfall and restoration machinery is unaffected.

issues.title: Before the operational questions: can the fund's own trust deed do this, and who pays when it goes wrong?
issues.plain_english: Two legal questions sit underneath everything else and neither has been asked. First, when the Tax Office directs the fund to release money to pay a member's tax bill, does the fund's own governing document actually permit the trustee to debit that member's interest and pay it out? Deeds were written before this tax existed. If a deed does not permit it, the fund needs a deed amendment before the first release notices arrive. The same question applies to recovering the cost of building the new system from members. Second, if a trustee gets the split wrong and a member suffers a tax detriment or a penalty, can the trustee reimburse itself out of the fund - that is, out of other members' money? Superannuation law limits when a trustee may be indemnified, particularly for penalties. If it can, the cost of a mistake made about a handful of very wealthy members is paid by everyone else. If it cannot, the trustee company's own capital is exposed to a liability it has never carried before.
issues.why_it_matters: These are threshold questions: if the answer to the first is no for a meaningful number of funds, an industry-wide deed amendment programme is needed before the first release notices, and nobody is running one. The second question is the sharper version of the cross-subsidy point, and it is the question the operational risk financial requirement analysis quietly assumes away - that reserve is itself members' money.

issues.title: Building this for a fraction of one per cent of members feeds a legislated pass/fail test that APRA itself administers
issues.plain_english: Even a fund with several million members may have fewer than about 1,500 members caught by this tax, yet it must build and run the whole capability. In dollars per member the cost is small - even on a generous assumption it is of the order of a dollar or two per member per year. The point is not the size of the cost; it is where it lands. If it is recovered through a flat administration fee, it feeds into the annual performance test, which compares a product's administration fees against the median for its category and combines that with investment performance. Fail by more than half a per cent two years running and the fund cannot take new members into that product. Because the benchmark is a median, the effect is uneven: a fund with a small affected population relative to its total membership carries the same fixed build cost over a smaller fee base. There is a perverse edge to this that is worth saying out loud - the test rewards absorbing, capitalising or quietly burying the cost over recovering it transparently from the members who generate it.
issues.why_it_matters: This converts a governance observation into a dated consequence in a regime APRA operates. It is also the kind of second-order effect that is obvious in hindsight and invisible at the time. FY2028 fee-setting is not yet locked in, so raising it now costs nothing.

issues.title: The Act also rewrites how every member's total balance is measured, and defined benefit members can lose the ability to contribute because of it
issues.plain_english: A second part of the Act changes how a person's total super is measured, and gives each separate pot of super its own value. That total is used for far more than this tax: it decides whether someone can put more money in, whether they can use unused contribution room from earlier years, and whether they qualify for government contributions. The change mainly affects defined benefit members, and the great majority of them will never pay this tax. Their measured balance can move because the measuring method changed, not because anything happened to their money. The concrete harm is easy to state: a member sees a lower reported balance, makes an extra contribution or a bring-forward election in reliance on it, and receives an excess contributions assessment. The fund is the entity that reports the number and the entity the member will ask.
issues.why_it_matters: This is the element most likely to be missed at executive level, because the whole debate is framed around a small high-balance cohort. It affects a far larger population, it is a disclosure and member-communication exposure that falls on trustees to explain, and the failure mode produces real financial detriment to ordinary members. The remedy - a reliable, well-explained published figure - largely sits with the Tax Office, which is why it is not graded higher.

issues.title: Members will ask their fund where they stand, and the fund cannot answer without a conflict
issues.plain_english: No single fund can tell a member whether this tax will catch them, because the threshold is measured across all of a person's super, including any self-managed fund. Only the Tax Office holds that view, and taxpayer confidentiality law is why the fund cannot be given it. But members will ask, and any answer risks being wrong. There is a sharper problem behind that. Because the first year turns on the balance at 30 June 2027, a fund that helpfully prompts its largest members about the deadline is prompting them to take money out of the fund - against its own revenue - and may be doing so with advice paid for collectively by members who receive nothing. A fund that says nothing leaves its largest members unserved and pushes them toward advisers who will recommend a self-managed fund. Every posture is exposed. Meanwhile the main industry body has asked that the trustee's 'fair and reasonable' split be put outside the reach of the external complaints scheme. Even if that were granted, members would keep their right to object to the Tax Office assessment - the question is whether that is a real remedy when the disputed judgement was made by someone else.
issues.why_it_matters: This is where a conduct failure is most likely to actually materialise, because it involves a fund talking to identified wealthy members about a dated decision under a direct conflict. It is joint APRA-ASIC territory rather than APRA's alone, which is why proximity is scored low. It also exposes a real impossibility under the retirement income covenant: the trustee must gather the information needed to formulate its strategy, and the decisive variable sits with the Tax Office.

issues.title: Perimeter: the capital gains reset favours SMALL funds - which includes some APRA-regulated ones - and the migration trend predates the tax
issues.plain_english: Small funds can make a one-off election to reset the tax cost of all their assets to market value at 30 June 2026, permanently removing gains built up before the tax started. Large funds get only a temporary discount that phases out. The important correction is that 'small' does not mean 'self-managed'. Small APRA funds - funds with no more than six members, trusteed by professional trustees APRA supervises - sit on the same side of the line. So a member can obtain the reset without leaving APRA's perimeter, and the design asymmetry is about fund size, not about who regulates the fund. The same six-member line means some of APRA's own licensees will attribute earnings by a completely different legal mechanism - a prescribed formula plus a compulsory annual actuarial certificate for every fund, every year, which is a real recurring cost for very small funds. On migration: net rollovers out of APRA-regulated funds into self-managed funds reached $12.2 billion in the year to March 2026, up 54 per cent. Whether this tax caused any of that is not established, and the largest single quarter was September 2025 - before the October 2025 redesign was announced.
issues.why_it_matters: The members most able to leave are the ones whose departure most erodes scale, and their fee contribution is disproportionate to their headcount where a percentage fee is capped. But this is squarely a Treasury design decision, not an APRA lever, and the causal story is not made out - which is why it is graded C. There is also a channel the analysis has missed entirely: a member can reduce their measured total by buying a lifetime income stream, and those are life company products that APRA also regulates. Part of what looks like a loss of perimeter is a transfer into another part of APRA's own house that has not been consulted.

issues.title: Post-death attribution is made law, not a draft - trustees must build to it, and it collides with the duty to pay death benefits promptly
issues.plain_english: When a member dies, the trustee must pay the death benefit as soon as practicable. Under the rules as made, fund earnings continue to be attributed to the deceased member's account until the death benefit is fully paid, and the liability may only be assessed after the money has gone - potentially leaving an estate with a tax bill and nothing left in super to pay it from. There is also an odd distinction: if the member had a pension that automatically continues to a spouse, attribution stops; if not, it continues. Identical families get different outcomes because of a paperwork choice. Three technical bodies contested this at consultation and it survived into the final regulations unchanged. That matters for what APRA says: these are not draft rules. Consultation closed on 7 April 2026, the regulations were made on 11 June and registered on 18 June 2026, and they first applied from 1 July 2026 (the start of the 2026-27 income year). Trustees must build to them.
issues.why_it_matters: Death benefits are already the most litigated area of superannuation. A trustee that pays promptly may strand a liability with an estate; a trustee that holds back to protect the estate risks breaching the cashing rule. There is no clean answer and executors will press trustees on both sides. It also injects a tax consideration into trustee discretion and into the advice members receive about death benefit nominations. It is graded C because the remedy is Treasury's, not APRA's, and the population is small.
instruments: Income Tax Assessment (1997 Act) Amendment Regulations 2026 (F2026L00726) Sch 1 (post-death attribution; 'death benefit income stream')
SIS Act and SIS Regulations cashing rules for death benefits (as soon as practicable)
SPS 521 Conflicts of Interest
SPS 515 member outcomes; internal dispute resolution obligations
issues.recommended_apra_position: Do NOT advise licensees to hold off building - the rule is made and operative, and telling supervised entities not to implement operative law would be wrong and potentially harmful. Instead, ask exposed licensees how they will reconcile continued post-death attribution with the obligation to cash death benefits as soon as practicable, and expect the tension to appear in complaints and in death benefit payment timeliness metrics. Separately, put the prudential consequence on the record with Treasury: post-death attribution conflicts with the cashing obligation, and the reversionary versus non-reversionary distinction rewards benefit design over substance. Confirm and communicate the final position, which is now determinable: no Division 296 liability arises in the year of death where death occurs on or before 30 June, with earnings then attributed to the undistributed interest until death benefits are fully paid.
issues.who_bears_it: Funds with large numbers of high-balance retirees; estates and legal personal representatives; beneficiaries, including in second-marriage fact patterns where estate and superannuation beneficiaries differ.
evidence_refs: LIKELIHOOD PROPOSITION: P(a trustee faces a live conflict between the cashing obligation and post-death attribution that produces a complaint, a delayed payment or estate detriment, in FY2028-29) = 3.

issues.title: This is not a system liquidity event - and here is the arithmetic that settles it
issues.plain_english: It is tempting to frame this as a risk that funds will be forced to sell assets in a hurry. The numbers do not support it. On APRA's own derivation, the annual amount drawn out of APRA-regulated funds is of the order of one per cent of the lump sums these funds already pay every year, and about three per cent of a single peak month in APRA's own stress test. The behavioural story does not hold either. For the first year only, whether a member pays depends on their balance at 30 June 2027, so in principle there is a deadline to get under three million. But a member at $3.2 million owes roughly $1,800 - nobody restructures a retirement portfolio and crystallises capital gains to avoid that. A member at eight or ten million has a bill worth managing, but cannot get under three million by any means short of destroying their position. The cohort with the incentive cannot act, and the cohort that can act has almost no incentive. Both tails argue against a rush. There is one residual point that is not about cash at all: because the tax falls on income received and gains realised, and not on growth left untouched, it gently rewards holding low-income, low-turnover assets - which points the same way as the growth in unlisted and private market holdings APRA has already flagged as a system risk.
issues.why_it_matters: Opening with a forced-sale narrative would repeat an argument the enacted law has already answered, and would cost credibility in the room. Stating the aggregate and behavioural position up front lets the meeting move to where the exposure actually is: operational, member-equity, third-party concentration and perimeter. The composition point is worth one paragraph because nobody else will raise it and it runs against, not with, APRA's stated system risk concern.
instruments: SPS 530 paras 31-38 (comprehensive investment stress testing programme at para 31; liquidity management plan and liquidity event at para 36)
SPG 530 paras 79(a) and 79(e) (member-generated events; policy-driven events)
SRS 553.0 (out-of-cycle valuation baseline from the December 2025 quarter)
APRA System Risk Stress Test framework
issues.recommended_apra_position: State the de minimis aggregate position explicitly at the top of the note, with the caveat that it is APRA's own derivation from a superseded-design revenue estimate, and put the per-member arithmetic ($1,800 / $9,000 / $63,000) alongside it. Then say clearly that the exposure is operational, member-equity, third-party concentration and perimeter - not liquidity - with two named exceptions: individual illiquid investment options, and licensees with concentrated high-balance membership. Keep the cheap test: ask materially exposed licensees to produce the SPG 530 para 79(e) policy-driven scenario for Division 296 covering the June 2027 quarter, and to confirm the liquidity management plan treats it as a liquidity event with defined actions. That is a low-cost, high-signal test of whether the plan is live, and it does not require the issue to be graded high. Add a monitoring line on portfolio composition against the SRS 553.0 baseline. Do not carry any 2023-vintage argument about unrealised gains, forced realisation, unusable paper losses or unindexed bracket creep into the meeting - all four were answered by the enacted design.
issues.who_bears_it: Nobody, in aggregate. Specific illiquid investment options and individual funds with concentrated high-balance membership remain exposed on a dispersion basis, as the 2020 early release episode showed.
evidence_refs: LIKELIHOOD PROPOSITION: P(Division 296-driven outflow produces a liquidity event at a material APRA-regulated fund in FY2027 or FY2028) = 2.

CREATED (own derivation, clearly labelled): Treasury's superseded-design costing implies roughly $28,750 of average annual liability per affected individual ($2.3bn in 2027-28 across about 80,000 individuals); applying the 31,800-of-80,000 APRA-side share gives an indicative $0.9bn a year, and less in practice. Against APRA-regulated lump sums of $79.7bn and assets of $3,141.1bn (year to March 2026), that is about 1.1% of annual lump sums and about 0.03% of assets, and about 3% of a single $30bn peak month in APRA's stress test. All comparisons use the same $0.9bn numerator. (The draft's 'one fifteenth of a peak month' mixed the whole-system numerator with the APRA-side one and is wrong.)

CREATED: the behavioural pricing above - $1,800 at $3.2m, $9,000 at $4m, $63,000 at $10m, on a 6% earnings assumption - is APRA's own arithmetic from the proportioning formula (TSB - $3m)/TSB. It is the single most useful number in the pack and should appear in the note.

There is an opposite-signed effect too: capital moving to SMSFs and direct holdings holds less unlisted infrastructure in aggregate than a large APRA-regulated fund does. Neither is measured; both belong in the note as analytical propositions.

framework_verdicts.instrument: CPS 230 Operational Risk Management - critical operations limb (paras 24, 35, 36(c), 38, 44)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Para 24 (VERIFIED verbatim): 'An APRA-regulated entity must manage its full range of operational risks, including but not limited to legal risk, regulatory risk, compliance risk, conduct risk, technology risk, data risk and change management risk.' Para 36(c) requires an RSE licensee to classify 'investment management and fund administration' as critical operations unless it can justify otherwise. Para 35 defines critical operations as processes undertaken by the entity 'or its service provider'. Para 38 requires tolerance levels for disruption time, data loss and minimum service levels. Para 44 requires severe-but-plausible scenario testing including 'disruptions to services provided by material service providers'. CORRECTION: the draft attributed the para 24 obligation to para 23; para 23 is senior management's duty to inform the Board.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: The Division 296 calculation, the attribution of earnings to members, the report to the Commissioner and any release-authority payment are all performed within fund administration, which is already a default critical operation. The externally set clocks (10 business days for defined benefit and certain other interests; 28 calendar days for other APRA-regulated funds) are hard deadlines set by a third party and cluster in a single annual window, so the operational risk is correlated across the industry rather than idiosyncratic. Note that para 35 expressly extends critical operations to processes performed by a service provider.

framework_verdicts.instrument: CPS 230 Operational Risk Management - service provider limb (paras 47-60, esp. 49, 50, 51, 59)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: VERIFIED from the in-force July 2025 standard. Para 47 requires a comprehensive service provider management policy. Para 49 requires the entity to 'identify and maintain a register of its material service providers', defined as 'those on which the entity relies to undertake a critical operation or that expose it to material operational risk'. Para 50 requires that, at a minimum, for an RSE licensee, providers of 'fund administration, custodial services, investment management and arrangements with promoters and financial planners' be classified as material service providers unless it can justify otherwise. Para 51: 'An APRA-regulated entity must submit its register of material service providers to APRA on an annual basis.' Paras 53-55 cover due diligence and formal agreements including APRA access rights; para 59 requires notification to APRA within 20 business days of entering or materially changing an agreement for a service supporting a critical operation. CORRECTION: the limb begins at para 47, not para 48 as the review assumed.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: This row was absent from the draft register and is the most consequential omission. The Division 296 calculation, attribution, reporting and release-authority payment will not be built independently by every licensee: they will be delivered largely by a small number of shared administrators, with custodians supplying the underlying income and realised-gain data, and external tax agents preparing the fund income tax return from which the fund earnings figure derives. Every one of those service types is a mandatory material service provider under para 50. Three consequences follow. First, a methodology defect or a build delay at one provider is a common-mode event affecting every client fund simultaneously, in the same annual window. Second, accountability is non-delegable: where an administrator computes the attribution, the licensee still owns the judgement, so a shared build means multiple boards adopting one vendor's method. Third, shared methodology cuts both ways - it produces consistency between funds sharing a provider and a step-change between blocs of funds using different ones. APRA does not need new data to map this: it already receives the material service provider register annually under para 51.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SPS 530 Investment Governance - stress testing and liquidity (paras 30-31, 36(d), 36(e), 38)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: VERIFIED. Para 30: 'An RSE licensee must have a comprehensive investment stress testing program that is approved by the Board and is integrated into an RSE licensee's investment governance framework.' Para 31 requires determination of appropriate adverse stress scenarios for the investment strategy of each option. Para 36 requires a Board-approved liquidity management plan for each RSE which, at 36(d), 'identifies the circumstances the RSE licensee considers to be a significantly adverse liquidity outcome that requires action (liquidity event)' and, at 36(e), 'outlines what action the RSE licensee will take when a liquidity event occurs'. Para 38 requires liquidity stress testing 'as part of the comprehensive investment stress testing program required in paragraph 31'. CORRECTION: the draft cited para 29 for the stress testing programme; para 29 concerns Board justification when amending an investment strategy. The standard's own cross-reference in para 38 points to para 31.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: The transitional first-year measurement date of 30 June 2027 and, from the following year, recurring release-authority outflows are both capable of being a liquidity event within para 36(d). The hook is well matched and no amendment is needed. The supervisory question is narrower and cheaper than an instrument change: whether any licensee has in fact run the scenario. Aggregate outflow is very unlikely to be a system liquidity event; residual exposure is confined to specific illiquid investment options and to licensees with concentrated high-balance membership.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SPG 530 Investment Governance - liquidity and policy-driven triggers (paras 79(a), 79(e), 92)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: VERIFIED verbatim. Para 79 lists liquidity stress factors a prudent RSE licensee would consider, including at 79(a) 'member generated events: changes in switching behaviour, redemptions and contributions' and at 79(e) 'policy driven events: a change in Government policy, for example, related to access to accrued member assets'. Para 92: APRA expects consideration of 'secondary risks associated with liquidity risk, including the impact of selling assets at stale prices, the impact on portfolio risk of an increasing proportion of illiquid assets and the cost of restoring the portfolio to the desired position.'
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Division 296 is close to the scenario the guidance already names. APRA can ask for the para 79(e) scenario today without any new instrument. The December 2024 thematic found wide reliance on a single illiquid-exposure trigger and limited monitoring of member outflow trends, which suggests the guidance exists but may not be being applied to this measure.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SPG 530 Investment Governance - member equity and valuation triggers (paras 9, 109, 110, 114)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: VERIFIED verbatim. Para 9: 'APRA expects an RSE licensee's investment governance framework would appropriately consider member equity risk with a view to all beneficiaries being dealt with fairly', including 'ensuring beneficiaries transact at fair prices across all investment options'. Para 109: APRA expects valuations at least quarterly. Para 110: 'An RSE licensee would consider triggers that would warrant more frequent valuations including market volatility and the external operating environment, including changes in Government policy settings.' Para 114: the valuation policy 'would also set out protocols for when and how the interim valuations are reviewed for appropriateness and to determine whether any adjustments or reversals need to be made for unit pricing purposes.'
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Attribution of fund earnings to individual members is a trustee-discretionary allocation that feeds a member's personal tax assessment. That is a member-equity matter under para 9 as much as a tax-compliance choice, and no current guidance says so. Division 296 also appears to be a 'changes in Government policy settings' trigger for the purposes of para 110, which APRA could confirm at low cost. This is the clearest candidate for a guidance update rather than a standard amendment.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SPS 530 Investment Governance - valuation governance framework (paras 39, 40, 41)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: VERIFIED. Para 39 requires an adequate valuation governance framework. Para 40 requires a Board-approved valuation policy covering, among other things, roles and responsibilities (40(a)), methodology by asset class (40(c)), circumstances for independent external valuations (40(d)), frequency having regard to 'member equity considerations' (40(e)), the circumstances in which interim valuations are made (40(f)) and 'the triggers that would require an interim valuation of investments outside of the frequency determined under paragraph 40(e)' (40(g)). Para 41 requires periodic Board review of valuation metrics.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Although tax on unrealised gains was removed from the final design, a member's balance at 30 June still determines both whether they are above the threshold and the proportion of earnings that is taxed. For members in unitised options that balance derives from the unit price, which derives from unlisted asset valuations. Valuation therefore remains relevant to an individual's tax outcome. APRA's December 2024 findings on conflicted valuation committee membership and assets not revalued for multiple quarters now carry a personal tax consequence for a small identifiable cohort, not only a unit-pricing consequence. Note the more likely complaint direction is upward revaluation lifting members over the threshold, which happens innocently, rather than downward suppression, which would require alleging misconduct and would harm every other member's exit price.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SPS 515 Strategic Planning and Member Outcomes (paragraph numbers not independently verified)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Requires a rolling business plan with financial projections across scenarios, prudent and transparent fee-setting, demonstrable purpose and funding source for expenditure, an annual business performance review assessing outcomes for member cohorts, and preparation for transfers in and out. Paragraph numbers cited in the draft register were not verified against the registered instrument in this pass and are omitted deliberately - two of the paragraph numbers that were checked elsewhere in the draft proved to be off by one.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Three distinct stresses. The business plan scenario set can accommodate Division 296 outflow without amendment. Build and run costs benefit well under one per cent of members but may be recovered from all of them through flat fees, which is a governed expenditure and fee-setting decision the board should be able to evidence. And a successor fund transfer spanning the 30 June 2027 measurement date has no settled protocol for transferring member-level Division 296 data, which places APRA's support for consolidation in tension with member-level tax accuracy. All are supervisable under the standard as drafted.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SPG 516 Business Performance Review
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: An RSE licensee has discretion to establish cohorts for the annual business performance review; APRA expects at least product-level cohorts. The guidance contemplates that 'separate cohorts may also be established using membership characteristics that cut across superannuation products, for example cohorts based on balance size'.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: High-balance members are already an assessable cohort under the existing guidance, but nothing names them. Naming them as an expected cohort would require trustees to assess whether outcomes for that cohort remain appropriate, and would surface any indifference to their departure - which is the mechanism by which scale, and therefore cost per remaining member, is eroded. This is one of the two strongest instrument-level options in the pack and is a low-cost guidance change rather than a standard amendment.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SPS 220 Risk Management (paragraph numbers not independently verified)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: The Board is ultimately responsible for the risk management framework; the framework must cover all material risks; a Board-approved risk appetite statement must set tolerances for each material risk category; and an annual risk management declaration is signed by two directors.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Division 296 implementation is simultaneously a regulatory, compliance, technology, data and change management risk within the meaning of CPS 230 para 24 (corrected from the draft's para 23), so it should be reflected in the risk appetite statement and stand behind the annual declaration. This is a signed, dated, director-level artefact APRA already receives, so it is an efficient place to test whether the risk has been genuinely assessed. Any supervisory expectation should be proportionate to the licensee's in-scope member population: a licensee with a handful of affected members that has not separately addressed Division 296 may have made a reasonable judgement rather than a governance failure.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SPS 114 Operational Risk Financial Requirement (paragraph numbers not independently verified)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Requires financial resources to protect beneficiaries against losses arising from operational risk, a Board-approved strategy, a target amount and tolerance limit reflecting the operational risk profile, and a replenishment plan if resources fall below tolerance.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: A mis-calculated or mis-attributed figure, or a release-authority payment made late or in the wrong amount, can produce a loss to a beneficiary and a penalty exposure - the kind of loss the requirement exists to absorb. Two questions sit underneath the sizing question and were not addressed in the draft: whether the reserve can lawfully be applied to compensate an individual's personal tax detriment, and whether a trustee can indemnify itself from fund assets for such an error, given the reserve is itself members' money. Those are legal questions that should be settled before the reserve is assumed to be the answer.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SPS 310 Audit and Related Matters (paragraph and attachment references not independently verified)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: The RSE auditor provides reasonable assurance over data reported under APRA reporting standards and over specified legislative compliance, and limited assurance over systems, controls and the effectiveness of the risk management framework.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Division 296 fund earnings and member attribution are reported to the Commissioner of Taxation, not under an APRA reporting standard, and arise under the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 and the Taxation Administration Act 1953 rather than the SIS Act. On the face of it they therefore fall outside both assurance limbs, meaning the largest new calculation many RSE licensees will perform carries no RSE auditor assurance. Amending SPS 310 would close this, but the proportionate first step is to ask what voluntary assurance licensees have obtained. An assurance gap on a high-consequence, member-specific calculation is a familiar precursor to a large remediation.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SIS Act s29JA breach notification (interaction with Division 296 obligations)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: An RSE licensee must notify APRA in writing where it has breached or will breach a condition of its licence and the breach is significant, with significance assessed by reference to inadequacies in the licensee's arrangements to ensure compliance with the RSE licensee law.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: The same reasoning that takes the Division 296 calculation outside RSE auditor assurance also takes it outside the ordinary breach-notification trigger: Division 296 duties arise under tax law, which is not RSE licensee law, so a late or materially wrong report to the Commissioner is unlikely of itself to be notifiable to APRA. It would become notifiable only derivatively, where it evidences inadequate compliance arrangements or causes member loss. The practical consequence is that APRA may learn of a systemic failure - including one originating at a shared administrator - late, or from the ATO rather than from the licensee. APRA has a recent precedent for closing exactly this kind of gap by stating an expectation in a letter: in its Payday Super Readiness letter of 25 March 2026 it told licensees that significant breaches of the new requirements would necessitate a breach notification under s29JA.

framework_verdicts.instrument: Taxation Administration Act 1953 Sch 1 ss 134-140 and 134-145 (new duties on superannuation providers)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Where the Commissioner keeps a Division 296 debt account for a member and the end benefit becomes payable, the provider must notify the Commissioner of the expected payment date within 14 days in the approved form (s 134-140). A material change in, or omission from, that notice must be corrected within 7 days (s 134-145). Section 134-140 carries an express note that a person dissatisfied may complain under the AFCA scheme.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: This is the clearest new positive duty the enacting legislation places on a fund, and it is a duty on a 'superannuation provider' - the term 'RSE licensee' does not appear in the enacting Act. The obligation is short-clock, event-driven and sits at the point where a benefit is being paid, so it lands in the same administration systems as the calculation and the release authority. The express AFCA note is significant for APRA's member-outcomes interest because it cuts against industry's request that Division 296 trustee judgements sit outside the external dispute resolution scheme. No APRA instrument change is available or needed; the relevance is to supervisory expectations about operational readiness and complaints capability.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SRS 611.0 Member Accounts (SRF 611.0 Instructions, Table 1 Column 3 and Table 2 Column 4)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: VERIFIED against the instrument. Members Benefit Bracket Type valid values run from '<$1,000' through '$100,000 to $199,999', '$200,000 to $499,999', '$500,000 to $999,999' and terminate at '$1,000,000+'. Data is reported per member account and separately for each RSE.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: The top bracket is one third of the lower Division 296 threshold and one tenth of the upper. APRA therefore cannot count members above $3 million or $10 million from its own collections, cannot see where they are concentrated, and cannot size the assets sitting behind them. A deeper limitation sits behind that: the threshold is measured on a person's total across every fund, including self-managed funds, whereas SRF 611.0 is keyed to the member account within a single RSE, so a member with $1.8 million in each of two funds appears twice below $2 million and never as a $3.6 million total. Additional brackets would materially improve visibility of large accounts in APRA-regulated funds but cannot by construction produce the whole-of-person threshold view, which only the ATO holds. Any external commitment should be framed as monitoring large-account behaviour in APRA-regulated funds rather than monitoring the affected population.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SRS 551.0 Liquidity (SRF 551.1 member cash flow items)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Quarterly reporting of liquidity supply, demand and event indicators. Member cash flows are reported on a net basis, without decomposition by driver.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: A release-authority payment, a Division 296-motivated rollover to a self-managed fund and an ordinary retirement lump sum are indistinguishable in the collection. APRA's newest liquidity collection therefore cannot isolate Division 296 outflow. Amending a collection that has only recently commenced would be disproportionate; a targeted, time-limited request to the most exposed licensees is the better route, and APRA can require data from named entities by written notice without making a new reporting standard - which also answers the timing objection that a standard cannot deliver before the first assessments issue.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SRS 553.0 Investment Exposure Concentrations and Valuations (SRF 553.1, SRF 553.3)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Quarterly reporting of out-of-cycle valuations for material unlisted investments and where there is material impact on investment options, plus an RSE valuation profile.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: None adverse - this is an asset rather than a gap, and it belongs alongside the SRS 611.0 shortfall so the picture is balanced. The collection commenced shortly before Division 296 began, giving APRA a clean pre-commencement baseline of out-of-cycle valuation frequency in precisely the asset class where any change in revaluation behaviour around 30 June 2027 would first appear. The opportunity is to use it deliberately as a comparison point rather than to collect anything further.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SPS 160 Defined Benefit Matters (paragraph numbers not independently verified)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Requires a Board-approved shortfall limit, periodic actuarial investigations, interim reporting to APRA where a fund moves into an unsatisfactory financial position, and a restoration plan within a set period.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Division 296 tax on a defined benefit interest is deferred to a debt account until the end benefit is paid, so there is no near-term call on fund solvency and the shortfall and restoration machinery are unaffected. No amendment is warranted. The stress is operational rather than prudential: an annual actuarial valuation of every member's entitlement using a method previously performed occasionally and largely by hand for family law purposes; a shorter response window than other funds; and a deferred liability that must be tracked for decades and survive mergers and administrator changes. For very small defined benefit plans the recurring actuarial cost may not be economic, which is a plausible trigger for wind-up and transfer and therefore a member-outcomes and supervisory-workload question. Note that the actuarial capability question should be analysed under CPS 230's service provider limb, not under SPS 231, which CPS 230 replaced from 1 July 2025.

framework_verdicts.instrument: CPS 234 Information Security
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Requires an information security capability commensurate with threats, assessment and control of information assets managed by third parties, systematic control testing, internal audit review, and notification to APRA within 72 hours of a material incident.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: The Division 296 dataset identifies, by name and by member, individuals with the largest superannuation balances in the country. It is assembled and transmitted largely by outsourced administrators and moves by bulk data exchange to the ATO. It is a high-value, third-party-managed information asset that did not exist before 1 July 2026 and may not yet appear in licensees' information asset registers or be classified at an appropriate sensitivity. The standard is adequate as drafted; the asset is new. Related and worth noting: the measure creates a foreseeable scam and misinformation vector aimed at the same cohort around the publicly known 30 June 2027 date, which is joint APRA, ASIC and ATO territory.

framework_verdicts.instrument: CPS 190 Recovery and Exit Planning
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Requires a recovery and exit plan appropriate to the entity's size, business mix and complexity, a trigger framework with early warning indicators, and credible recovery actions.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Sustained loss of the highest-balance cohort reduces funds under management and average account balance, pressuring the cost base. The mechanism is sharper than generic scale erosion: where a fund charges a percentage-based administration fee with a dollar cap, members above the cap pay the maximum fee while consuming ordinary servicing cost, so they are net contributors to fixed costs and their departure removes revenue disproportionately to headcount. Most discussion assumes large funds, but the tail risk sits with small licensees whose membership skews high-balance, where losing a few hundred large accounts is a scale event. This is supervisable through the existing trigger framework without amendment.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SPS 250 Insurance in Superannuation
