framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Requires an insurance management framework and strategy, premium cost recovery arrangements, and demonstration to APRA that rules for attributing status to a beneficiary are fair and reasonable.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Tested and cleared. Premium erosion is immaterial for members above the thresholds. Two second-order effects exist - a member who withdraws to reduce a balance may fall toward levels where cover lapses, and death benefit insurance proceeds can temporarily inflate a balance - but neither warrants supervisory reprioritisation. Recorded so that the framework review can be shown to be complete: naming what is not affected is as useful to the meeting as naming what is.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SIS Act s52(2) covenants - best financial interests and fair and equitable treatment
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Trustees must perform their duties and exercise their powers in the best financial interests of beneficiaries, and must deal with members fairly as between members and classes of member.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: The covenants are a real but blunt constraint on the attribution judgement. Different defensible methods redistribute between members rather than making everyone better off, so 'best financial interests' and fair treatment do not by themselves select a single method. If APRA wants consistency it must give guidance or accept divergence. One caution on framing: a trustee cannot breach the equitable treatment covenant merely by applying a differential basis that Parliament has prescribed - for example the different treatment of defined benefit and accumulation interests. That is a communications challenge for trustees, not a trustee equity failing. The covenant bites where the trustee actually has discretion, which is the attribution method itself.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SIS Act s52(6) investment strategy covenant
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Requires the trustee to formulate, review regularly and give effect to an investment strategy having regard to the whole of the circumstances of the entity, including the liquidity of investments having regard to expected cash flow requirements.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Once assessments and release authorities begin, those payments become an expected cash flow requirement, so a strategy review that omits them would be incomplete. The covenant and the SPS 530 liquidity management plan point the same way, so APRA is not stretching either. Timing is favourable: first outflows follow the first assessments, giving two full investment strategy review cycles to prepare.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SIS Act s52(8A) and s52AA retirement income covenant; SPS 515 retirement income strategy requirement
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Requires the trustee to formulate, review regularly and give effect to a retirement income strategy, and to take reasonable steps to gather the information necessary to inform its formulation and review.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Drawing down reduces a member's balance and therefore future liability, creating a tax-driven incentive to draw faster or to hold assets outside superannuation - for exactly the cohort the covenant targets, most of whom are in or near retirement phase. It also exposes a genuine impossibility: the trustee must gather the information needed to inform the strategy, but the decisive variable is the member's balance across all funds, which only the ATO holds and which taxpayer confidentiality restricts it from sharing. Making Division 296 a named question in retirement income strategy reviews is a proportionate guidance response; the information asymmetry needs a legislative remedy rather than a prudential one.

framework_verdicts.instrument: Joint APRA-ASIC unit pricing good practice guidance; ASIC RG 94 (unit pricing)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Good practice expectations for unit pricing, including the treatment of tax provisions at investment option level, and for error correction and remediation.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Industry has itself nominated unit pricing and crediting rate governance as the right analogue for a 'fair and reasonable' attribution, and it is the one domain where APRA and ASIC have joint experience of pricing errors and remediation. Two limitations should be stated. First, this is jointly ASIC's territory, so any update is a joint product rather than an APRA one. Second, the analogy does not reach the whole sector: a material part of the APRA-regulated population, concentrated in the public sector and corporate schemes that are among the most exposed, uses periodic and often smoothed crediting rates rather than unit pricing, with the smoothing funded through reserves. Attributing realised earnings in a smoothed crediting-rate fund is a materially harder problem and the unit pricing analogy does not answer it.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SPS 521 Conflicts of Interest
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Requires a conflicts management framework covering the identification, avoidance and management of conflicts of interests and conflicts of duty.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Three conflicts are worth examining, none of which was assessed at paragraph level in this work, so the verdict is provisional. Tax management decisions - when to realise gains, how to sequence disposals - now affect identified individuals' personal tax, creating a weak incentive to favour a small cohort. Where an RSE licensee sits in a group that also owns self-managed fund administration, platform or advice businesses, the group has a commercial interest in the very migration that erodes the licensee's scale. And any trustee communication to high-balance members about the 30 June 2027 date is a prompt with a foreseeable one-way outcome, given that acting on it reduces the trustee's own funds under management. That last point is joint APRA-ASIC territory and is the most likely place a conduct issue actually materialises.

framework_verdicts.instrument: SPS 510 Governance and SPS 520 Fit and Proper (not examined at paragraph level)
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Govern Board composition, skills, committee structures and the fitness and propriety of responsible persons. Neither standard was examined at paragraph level in this work and no paragraph numbers are asserted.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Included because the central recommendation elsewhere in this note - that the attribution methodology be Board-approved - depends on these standards and the draft register never checked them. Three answerable questions follow: whether the Board skills matrix contemplates the capability needed to approve a methodology that drives individual members' tax outcomes; which Board committee owns it, given that on this characterisation the audit committee may assume the investment committee has it and vice versa; and what Board approval means in substance where the methodology originates with a shared administrator and is adopted rather than formed. Low confidence and flagged as a completeness item rather than a finding.

framework_verdicts.instrument: CPS 900 Resolution Planning
framework_verdicts.current_requirement: Applies to RSE licensees; resolution planning is triggered by the prospect of entity failure.
framework_verdicts.div296_stress: Examined and cleared. No defensible link was established: resolution planning is triggered by failure, and Division 296 does not create a failure pathway distinct from the gradual scale erosion already captured under CPS 190. Recorded so that the framework review can be represented as complete rather than selective.

open_consultation_asks: FRAMING NOTE FOR ALL OF THE BELOW. Both Treasury consultations on this measure have closed (exposure draft, and draft regulations closed 7 April 2026), so there is no open public process to lodge a submission into. The Government's October 2025 commitment to further consultation on how realised earnings are calculated and attributed is being progressed through an ATO co-design process, and APRA engages bilaterally with both Treasury and the ATO. These are therefore points to carry into that existing engagement and into the ATO's co-design work as guidance products are developed - an opportunity to add a prudential and member-outcomes perspective to work that is already under way, not a gap in anyone's current practice.

OFFER A PRUDENTIAL PERSPECTIVE ON THE GOVERNANCE OF ATTRIBUTION, WITHOUT PRESCRIBING THE TAX METHOD. The method by which a fund attributes earnings to individual members is being settled through ATO guidance. APRA's distinctive contribution is not the arithmetic but the governance wrapper: that the choice of method is a member-equity decision within the investment governance framework, and so warrants a written and Board-approved methodology, applied consistently from year to year, documented well enough to be reproduced for the full amendment period, and subject to some form of independent review. Worth noting that industry has itself proposed governance by analogy to unit pricing and crediting rate practice. Also worth putting: a default or safe-harbour method that a trustee adopting it can rely on would do more to produce consistent member outcomes than any governance expectation APRA could set, and industry would likely support it - but the design of any such method is properly the ATO's and Treasury's call.

RECORD THE THIRD-PARTY CONCENTRATION CONSEQUENCE. The calculation, attribution, reporting and payment functions will be delivered not by each licensee independently but largely by a small number of shared administrators and custodians - all of them mandatory material service providers under CPS 230 para 50. The prudential consequence worth putting on the record with the ATO is that a defect or delay at one provider is a common-mode event across many funds simultaneously, in the same annual window, rather than an isolated failure. This is relevant to how the ATO sequences its information requests, how much transition support it plans, and how it handles first-year extensions. APRA can inform this from the material service provider registers it already receives annually.

SETTLE THE TRANSFER PROTOCOL BEFORE THE FY2027 MERGER SEASON. The protocol for carrying member-level Division 296 information through a successor fund transfer or intra-fund transfer needs to be settled for transfers spanning the 30 June 2027 measurement date. This is squarely APRA's business because APRA actively encourages consolidation, so an unresolved protocol means APRA's own consolidation agenda could generate member-level tax errors. (The earlier industry discussion of a 'retrospective law' problem related to the abandoned 1 July 2025 commencement under the previous design and no longer applies: Royal Assent on 13 March 2026 preceded commencement on 1 April 2026.)

ASK FOR A CURRENT IN-SCOPE HEADCOUNT, SPLIT BY SECTOR. The only Commonwealth estimate of the affected population was struck under the superseded design on older data, and no absolute headcount has been published for the enacted realised-earnings design. Without a current number split between APRA-regulated funds, exempt public sector schemes and self-managed funds, APRA cannot calibrate supervisory intensity, cannot test a licensee that says it has very few affected members, and cannot size the perimeter question. This is a low-cost ask and the ATO is the only party that can answer it.

RESOLVE THE LEGAL GATEWAY BEFORE PURSUING A DATA EXCHANGE. A standing ATO-to-APRA data exchange covering balance distribution and Division 296 outflows by fund would substantially answer APRA's visibility problem without any change to APRA's own collections. The threshold question is whether taxpayer confidentiality in the taxation administration law permits it, and whether the existing APRA-ATO arrangements cover it or an amendment is needed. That question should be settled first, because if the answer is no, the remedy is a legislative one for Treasury rather than an administrative one for the ATO. Note also that the Council of Financial Regulators does not include the ATO, so this is a bilateral matter rather than a CFR one.

PUT THE CHANGE-SATURATION POINT ON THE RECORD. Payday Super and Division 296 commenced on the same day, in the same administration systems, drawing on the same finite pool of administrator change capacity, with Payday Super carrying the earlier and more visible deadline. The foreseeable consequence is that Division 296 is the change most likely to be deprioritised - and it is the one with guidance still being developed, no external assurance, and a multi-year amendment tail. This is worth stating to Treasury and the ATO as a sequencing and transition-support consideration, and it is directly relevant to how much first-year flexibility the ATO builds in.

RECORD PRUDENTIAL AND MEMBER-OUTCOMES CONSEQUENCES, LEAVING THE REMEDIES TO THE POLICY OWNER. Several contested design features have real consequences for supervised entities and their members, but the remedies are tax design questions for Treasury and the ATO and APRA should not advocate specific tax mechanics. The consequences worth recording are: (a) continued attribution of earnings after a member's death sits awkwardly with the trustee's obligation to cash a death benefit as soon as practicable, and trustees will need to know which obligation yields - noting that this rule is now made law, so licensees must build to it rather than wait; (b) where a fund amends its income tax return, the resulting re-reporting can reopen personal assessments years later, which is an administrative and record-keeping burden on trustees disproportionate to the typically small change in any member's tax; (c) the cost-base transitional treatment differs by fund size rather than by regulator, so some APRA-regulated entities sit on each side of the line, and the asymmetry is a migration incentive worth monitoring rather than a settled cause of the recent rollover trend; and (d) industry has asked that trustee attribution judgements sit outside the external dispute resolution scheme - APRA should have a view before this is settled by default, noting that the new notification duty on providers in the taxation administration law carries an express note preserving AFCA complaints, which cuts against that request, and that the question is primarily ASIC's and Treasury's perimeter.

audit_trail.assertion: Division 296 of the ITAA 1997 is enacted law: Treasury Laws Amendment (Building a Stronger and Fairer Super System) Act 2026 and Superannuation (Building a Stronger and Fairer Super System) Imposition Act 2026, Royal Assent 13 March 2026, first applies from 1 July 2026 (the start of the 2026-27 income year), first measurement date 30 June 2027.
audit_trail.basis: Enacting Acts as registered (C2026A00008 and the companion Imposition Act); Parliamentary Library Bills Digest No. 48, 2025-26. Established and independently confirmed in the workflow's settled-facts list. The Imposition Act is what fixes the rates and must be named alongside the amending Act.

audit_trail.assertion: The design is an additional 15% on earnings attributable to a Total Superannuation Balance above $3m (30% headline) and an additional 25% above $10m (40% headline); both thresholds are indexed; the base is realised earnings; unrealised gains were removed from the 2023 design; the tax is assessed on the individual, not the fund, with a release authority to draw it from superannuation.
audit_trail.basis: Treasury fact sheet 'Better Targeted Superannuation Concessions', 13 October 2025 (https://treasury.gov.au/publication/p2025-709385-btsc); Bills Digest No. 48. Settled in the workflow's verified-facts list.

audit_trail.assertion: Subdivision 296-A of the ITAA 1997 contains only s 296-5, an objects clause, and imposes no obligation on any person.
audit_trail.basis: Compiled ITAA 1997, Compilation No. 266, compilation date 1 July 2026. Independently verified prior to this pass. Consequence for the note: no obligation on trustees can be sourced to Subdivision 296-A, and any earlier draft language implying otherwise has been removed.

audit_trail.assertion: The term 'RSE licensee' does not appear anywhere in the enacting Act; the Act uses 'superannuation provider'.
audit_trail.basis: Full-text check of the enacting Act, independently verified prior to this pass. The note therefore describes duties as falling on 'superannuation providers', and states expressly that APRA's supervised population is a subset of that term rather than its referent.

audit_trail.assertion: The clearest new duty the regime places on a fund is s 134-140 of Schedule 1 to the Taxation Administration Act 1953: where the Commissioner keeps a Division 296 debt account for a member and the end benefit becomes payable, the provider must notify the Commissioner of the expected payment date within 14 days, in the approved form.
audit_trail.basis: s 134-140 Sch 1 TAA 1953 as enacted; independently verified prior to this pass. This replaces the draft register's unsupported framing that no instrument imposes a fund-side duty.

audit_trail.assertion: s 134-145 of Schedule 1 to the TAA 1953 requires a material change or omission in that notification to be corrected within 7 days.
audit_trail.basis: s 134-145 Sch 1 TAA 1953 as enacted; independently verified prior to this pass.

audit_trail.assertion: s 134-140 carries an express note that a person dissatisfied with the provider's conduct may complain under the AFCA scheme.
audit_trail.basis: Express note to s 134-140 Sch 1 TAA 1953; independently verified prior to this pass.

audit_trail.assertion: That express AFCA note cuts against the industry request that trustee Division 296 judgements be placed outside external dispute resolution.
audit_trail.basis: Chain: (1) ASFA's 7 April 2026 submission asks that 'fair and reasonable' estimates be 'outside of the scope of matters subject to AFCA review'; (2) Parliament, in the same reform package, attached an express AFCA note to the principal new provider-facing duty; (3) an express statutory note contemplating AFCA complaints about provider conduct under this regime is evidence Parliament assumed AFCA jurisdiction rather than excluding it. The inference is about parliamentary assumption, not about AFCA's jurisdictional source, which lies in the Corporations Act and the AFCA Rules.

audit_trail.assertion: For funds with more than six members the attribution of Division 296 fund earnings to individual members is on a 'fair and reasonable' basis with the method left to the trustee; funds with six or fewer members use a prescribed formula plus an annual actuarial certificate.
audit_trail.basis: Bills Digest No. 48, 2025-26; ASFA submission to Treasury, 7 April 2026; practitioner analyses of the draft regulations. The operative text in F2026L00726 could not be read directly (the Federal Register serves documents through a JavaScript front end), so this rests on secondary description of the instrument rather than the instrument itself.

audit_trail.assertion: The final regulations, Income Tax Assessment (1997 Act) Amendment Regulations 2026 (F2026L00726), were made 11 June 2026 and registered 18 June 2026 - thirteen days before the first measurement year began.
audit_trail.basis: Federal Register of Legislation, F2026L00726 'as made' metadata (https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2026L00726/asmade). Registration and making dates are readable from the register listing even where the instrument text is not.

audit_trail.assertion: The elective 30 June 2026 cost-base reset is available to small funds - SMSFs and small APRA funds - not to SMSFs alone; large funds and pooled superannuation trusts receive only a declining prescribed-factor method over four years.
audit_trail.basis: Income Tax (Transitional Provisions) Act 1997 Division 296 transitional provisions as described in Bills Digest No. 48 and in the Tax Institute submission; the small-fund boundary was raised by red-team review. Not read against the operative transitional text. Material because small APRA funds are inside APRA's perimeter, which weakens a pure 'migration out of the perimeter' framing.

audit_trail.assertion: Post-death attribution of earnings survived into the made regulations; the earlier recommendation that licensees should not build to it has been removed as wrong.
audit_trail.basis: Practitioner commentary on release of the made regulations reporting no change to post-death earnings treatment and the introduction of a 'death benefit income stream' concept, raised in red-team review. Primary text not read. The corrected position - the rule is operative law and licensees must build to it - is stated in the note; the reconciliation of post-death attribution with the duty to cash death benefits as soon as practicable is put as a supervisory question, not as an instruction to disregard the instrument.

audit_trail.assertion: CPS 230 paragraph 24, not paragraph 23, requires an entity to manage its full range of operational risks including legal, regulatory, compliance, conduct, technology, data and change management risk; paragraph 23 is senior management's duty to inform the Board.
audit_trail.basis: Prudential Standard CPS 230 Operational Risk Management, in-force July 2025 version, read verbatim. Independently verified prior to this pass. The register's off-by-one appeared in five places and has been corrected throughout.

audit_trail.assertion: CPS 230 paragraph 36(c) makes investment management and fund administration default critical operations for an RSE licensee unless the licensee can justify otherwise; paragraphs 35, 38 and 44 (tolerance levels and business continuity testing) apply accordingly.
audit_trail.basis: CPS 230 in-force July 2025 version, paragraphs read verbatim.

audit_trail.assertion: CPS 230 also carries a service provider management limb, and APRA already holds a completed material service provider register from every superannuation trustee, submitted by 1 October 2025, collected for the stated purpose of identifying concentration risk across the sector.
audit_trail.basis: APRA, 'APRA releases material service provider register template' (https://www.apra.gov.au/news-and-publications/apra-releases-material-service-provider-register-template) - confirmed this pass: registers due from ADIs, superannuation trustees and insurers by 1 October 2025, purpose includes identifying where multiple entities rely on a single provider. APRA also finalised targeted CPS 230 amendments on 30 April 2026.

audit_trail.assertion: SPS 231 Outsourcing was revoked on 1 July 2025 and its subject matter absorbed into CPS 230; citing SPS 231 in 2026 is an error and the defined benefit actuarial outsourcing question runs under CPS 230's service provider requirements.
audit_trail.basis: APRA Prudential Handbook and CPS 230 response materials - confirmed this pass that CPS 230 came into effect 1 July 2025 replacing CPS/SPS 231 Outsourcing and 232 Business Continuity Management.

audit_trail.assertion: The comprehensive investment stress testing programme is SPS 530 paragraph 31, not paragraph 29; SPS 530 paragraph 38 cross-refers to 'paragraph 31'.
audit_trail.basis: SPS 530 Investment Governance, read via the integrated SPS/SPG 530 text; para 38 self-referentially confirms para 31. Independently verified prior to this pass. Paragraph 29 concerns Board justification for amending an investment strategy.

audit_trail.assertion: SPS 530 paragraphs 36(d) and 36(e) require the liquidity management plan to identify a liquidity event and the action to be taken; paragraphs 39-41 establish the valuation governance framework, including triggers for interim valuations.
audit_trail.basis: SPS 530 Investment Governance, paragraphs read verbatim from the integrated text.

audit_trail.assertion: SPG 530 paragraph 9 states APRA's expectation that member equity risk be considered with a view to all beneficiaries being dealt with fairly; paragraph 79(e) names 'policy driven events: a change in Government policy, for example, related to access to accrued member assets'; paragraph 110 names 'changes in Government policy settings' as a trigger for more frequent valuations.
audit_trail.basis: Prudential Practice Guide SPG 530 Investment Governance, integrated version (https://www.apra.gov.au/system/files/2023-07/Prudential%20Practice%20Guide%20SPG%20530%20Investment%20Governance%20Integrated%20version%20-%20clean.pdf).

audit_trail.assertion: SPG 516 already permits cohorts based on balance size, so high-balance members can be named as an expected cohort in the annual business performance review without amending a prudential standard.
audit_trail.basis: SPG 516 Business Performance Review: 'Separate cohorts may also be established using membership characteristics that cut across superannuation products, for example cohorts based on balance size.'

audit_trail.assertion: RSE auditor assurance under SPS 310 does not currently reach the Division 296 calculation and attribution.
audit_trail.basis: Chain: (1) SPS 310 Attachment A directs reasonable assurance at data reported under APRA reporting standards and Attachment B at specified legislative compliance; (2) Division 296 fund earnings and member attribution are reported to the Commissioner under the ITAA 1997 and TAA 1953, not under any APRA reporting standard, and do not arise under the SIS Act; (3) therefore neither assurance limb reaches the calculation. Stated in the note as an assurance gap to be tested by asking what voluntary assurance licensees have obtained, not as a proposal to amend SPS 310.

audit_trail.assertion: A late, incomplete or materially wrong Division 296 report to the Commissioner is not, of itself, a breach notifiable to APRA under SIS Act s 29JA; it becomes notifiable only derivatively, where it evidences inadequate compliance arrangements or produces member loss.
audit_trail.basis: Chain: (1) s 29JA keys significant-breach notification to breaches of licence conditions, assessed by reference to arrangements to comply with the RSE licensee law and Chapter 2M of the Corporations Act; (2) Division 296 obligations arise under the ITAA 1997 and TAA 1953, which are not RSE licensee law; (3) so the direct trigger is absent. The s 29JA text was not read verbatim in this pass, so the legal premise should be confirmed by APRA Legal before the note is relied on externally. The recommended fix - stating an expectation of notification in a letter - does not depend on resolving it.

audit_trail.assertion: APRA has an immediate, four-month-old precedent for the intervention recommended here: its 'Payday Super Readiness' letter to RSE licensees of March 2026, which told licensees to revisit implementation timelines, stated that APRA would expect contribution processing to be a CPS 230 critical operation, and stated that significant breaches of the new requirements would necessitate a breach notification to APRA.
audit_trail.basis: APRA, 'Payday Super Readiness' (https://www.apra.gov.au/payday-super-readiness) - content confirmed this pass, including the three-business-day allocation requirement from 1 July 2026, the ATO's concern that a material number of licensees were not on track for SuperStream 3.0 Member Verification Request, and the CPS 230 and breach-notification statements.

audit_trail.assertion: Payday Super and Division 296 commence on the same day, 1 July 2026, and land on the same administration platforms, data pipelines and finite administrator change capacity; Payday Super carries the earlier and more visible deadline, so Division 296 is the change more likely to be deprioritised.
audit_trail.basis: Chain: (1) both measures first apply from 1 July 2026 (APRA Payday Super Readiness letter; Division 296 commencement); (2) both are delivered through fund administration and registry systems, which CPS 230 para 36(c) treats as a critical operation; (3) Payday Super has a daily, visible, employer-facing deadline while Division 296 has no external test until the ATO's first information requests in 2027-28; (4) scarce change capacity is therefore allocated to the visible deadline. Behavioural claim, not measured.

audit_trail.assertion: APRA engages bilaterally with Treasury and the ATO, and the remaining calculation and attribution work is progressing through an ATO co-design process; the opportunity is to contribute a prudential perspective to that work, not to remedy an exclusion.
audit_trail.basis: Established and confirmed in the workflow's settled-facts list. The published membership page for the ATO Superannuation Administration Group does not list APRA, but a published stakeholder-group membership list is not evidence of the full engagement channel, and the note no longer asserts that APRA has 'no voice' or is 'not in the room'.

audit_trail.assertion: As at 26 July 2026 APRA has published no Division 296-specific letter, guide, FAQ or speech.
audit_trail.basis: Domain-restricted searches of apra.gov.au; the Chair's June 2026 Senate opening statement does not mention the measure. This is a search-based negative finding, not an exhaustive check of APRA's internal publication index, and should be confirmed internally before being stated externally.

audit_trail.assertion: APRA's highest published member benefit bracket is '$1,000,000+', which is one third of the lower threshold; at 31 March 2026 that bracket held 305,000 accounts (1.28% of accounts) and $441.5bn of members' benefits (13.8%), with an average balance in the bracket of $1.45m.
audit_trail.basis: Reporting Standard SRS 611.0 Member Accounts, SRF 611.0 Instructions Table 1 Column 3; APRA Quarterly Superannuation Industry Publication, March 2026, Table 8.

audit_trail.assertion: An average balance of $1.45m against a $1m floor implies a steeply decaying right tail, so the population above $3m in APRA-regulated funds is small - most likely in the hundreds per large licensee rather than the thousands.
audit_trail.basis: Chain: (1) the $1m+ bracket averages $1.45m across 305,000 accounts; (2) an average only 45% above the floor is inconsistent with a heavy tail; (3) that is consistent with Treasury's estimate of roughly 31,800 affected individuals across all APRA-regulated funds and exempt public sector schemes; (4) spread across the large-licensee population this implies hundreds per fund. Presented in the note as APRA's own inference used to calibrate supervisory intensity, and as the reason a per-licensee in-scope headcount should be obtained.

audit_trail.assertion: An affected member's liability is small near the lower threshold: on a 6% earnings assumption, roughly $1,800 at a $3.2m balance, roughly $9,000 at $4m and roughly $63,000 at $10m, because only the proportion of earnings referable to the balance above $3m is taxed.
audit_trail.basis: Own arithmetic from the enacted proportioning mechanic (taxed proportion = (TSB - $3m)/TSB) and a stated 6% earnings assumption, generated for this meeting because no source publishes worked per-member amounts. Labelled in the note as APRA's own illustration with the assumption shown. It is the calibration figure against which the behavioural and materiality judgements in the note should be tested.

audit_trail.assertion: Aggregate Division 296 outflow is not a system liquidity event: an indicative APRA-side liability of about $0.9bn a year is roughly 1.1% of annual lump sum payments, about 0.03% of assets, and about 3% of a single peak month in APRA's own system stress test.
audit_trail.basis: Own derivation, clearly labelled: Treasury's superseded-design costing of $2.3bn in 2027-28 across ~80,000 individuals, scaled by the 31,800-of-80,000 APRA-side share, against APRA-regulated lump sums of $79.7bn and assets of $3,141.1bn for the year to March 2026. The earlier 'one fifteenth of a peak month' figure was wrong - it mixed a whole-of-system numerator with an APRA-side comparison - and has been corrected to a single consistent numerator. Rests on a superseded-design revenue estimate, so it bounds the order of magnitude only.

audit_trail.assertion: APRA's inaugural System Risk Stress Test modelled $174bn of cumulative liquidity demand, just under 16% of net assets, with peak monthly calls of about $30bn, and funds largely avoided selling unlisted assets, meeting the shock primarily through listed holdings.
audit_trail.basis: APRA System Risk Stress Test, 30 June 2026 (https://www.apra.gov.au/news-and-publications/system-risk-stress-test). Wording corrected from the draft's categorical 'without selling a single unlisted asset', which the source does not support.

audit_trail.assertion: APRA's December 2024 thematic reviewed 23 RSE licensees holding $2,018bn and 18.7m member accounts, and found 12 require material improvement in valuation governance, liquidity risk management or both; the eight-licensee liquidity subgroup represents 27% of funds under management and 5.4m member accounts.
audit_trail.basis: APRA, 'Governance of unlisted asset valuation and liquidity risk management in superannuation', 17 December 2024. Corrected: the $2,018bn and 18.7m figures are the scope of the review, not the size of the 12 licensees requiring improvement, as the draft register implied.

audit_trail.assertion: The December 2024 findings bear on general governance capacity in the platform and mid-sized cohort; they are not evidence of unreadiness for the Division 296 calculation, which sits in different systems and teams.
audit_trail.basis: Chain: (1) the thematic assessed unlisted asset valuation governance and liquidity risk frameworks, which are investment operations functions; (2) Division 296 calculation and attribution sit in tax and member administration; (3) therefore the thematic is indicative of governance capacity, not probative of Division 296 readiness. The sound reason for prioritising platform and wrap trustees is that member-directed options make attribution genuinely divergent, since members' assets are individually identifiable.

audit_trail.assertion: CSS Fund reports 23.58% of its accounts above $1m and is used as a named concentration in the exposed-cohort analysis.
audit_trail.basis: Derived from APRA Quarterly Superannuation Fund Statistics, March 2026, Table 3. Contested: the same reporting entity's figures for PSS and MilitarySuper show fewer than 20 accounts above $1m against average balances near $585,000 and $546,000, which looks like a reporting artefact. The note carries CSS as 'subject to data verification' and the derived headline that CSS alone holds 7.9% of all $1m+ accounts has been withdrawn pending confirmation with Commonwealth Superannuation Corporation.

audit_trail.assertion: Net rollovers from APRA-regulated funds to SMSFs were $12.2bn in the year to March 2026, up 53.8% on $7.9bn a year earlier.
audit_trail.basis: APRA Quarterly Superannuation Performance Statistics to March 2026, Table 1a.

audit_trail.assertion: That rollover growth cannot be attributed to Division 296.
audit_trail.basis: Chain: (1) the largest single quarter in the series is September 2025, which precedes the 13 October 2025 redesign announcement; (2) the strongest available establishment data attributes SMSF growth to demand for direct control and lower online setup costs, with new funds skewing to ages 35-44 - the opposite demographic; (3) therefore the trend predates the measure and causation is not established. The legislated cost-base asymmetry is a genuine incentive and is stated separately; the flow series is carried as a monitoring line, not as evidence of effect.

audit_trail.assertion: Treasury estimated 31,800 of approximately 80,000 affected individuals would sit in APRA-regulated funds and exempt public sector schemes.
audit_trail.basis: Office of Impact Analysis, 'Impact Analysis: Better Targeted Superannuation Concessions', Treasury, January 2024. Contested on two grounds: it was struck on 2022-vintage data under the superseded change-in-balance design, and it combines APRA-regulated funds with exempt public sector schemes, which are not APRA-supervised - so it overstates APRA's own exposure by an unknown margin. Carried in the note with both caveats attached, as the only Commonwealth figure available.

audit_trail.assertion: The whole-of-person threshold cannot be produced from any APRA collection, because SRS 611.0 is reported per RSE and keyed on member account rather than person; only the ATO holds the aggregated view.
audit_trail.basis: Chain: (1) SRS 611.0 requires reporting separately for each RSE; (2) SRF 611.0 is keyed on member account; (3) a member with $1.8m in each of two APRA-regulated funds appears twice below $2m and never as a $3.6m total; (4) therefore adding balance brackets improves large-account visibility but structurally cannot produce the threshold view. This is why the note frames any external commitment as monitoring large-account behaviour in APRA-regulated funds, not monitoring the affected population.

audit_trail.assertion: The ATO's indicative information-request windows are 10 business days for defined benefit and alternative-method interests and 28 calendar days for other APRA-regulated funds.
audit_trail.basis: ATO Superannuation Administration Group key messages, 18 February 2026 and 20 May 2026. Contested: the February meeting records DB requests from November 2027 and APRA-fund requests from February 2028, while the May meeting says November and April with no year stated, and neither reconciles cleanly with assessments issuing in the second half of 2027-28. Cited in the note as ATO indicative planning dates that have already moved once, not as settled deadlines.

audit_trail.assertion: The ATO intends to reuse existing Division 293 SuperStream product type codes for Division 296 release authorities, distinguished by a reference number rather than a new message type.
audit_trail.basis: ATO Superannuation Administration Group key messages of 17 June 2025 - re-dated after review established that the 2026 SAG pages the draft cited do not contain this text. Contested as an APRA ask: ASFA's 7 April 2026 submission expressly asked the ATO to build on the Division 293 release channel and messaging on cost-to-members grounds, so the note discloses industry's position and seeks a machine-readable flag on the existing message rather than a new message type.

audit_trail.assertion: The ten-business-day payment clock and 20-penalty-unit exposure for release authorities are the existing obligations for other release authority types; the Division 296 equivalent has not been published.
audit_trail.basis: ATO release authority guidance for APRA-regulated funds, which lists six release authority categories and does not yet include Division 296. The note states the position this way in plain English rather than asserting a ten-day Division 296 deadline as settled.

audit_trail.assertion: Division 296 build and run costs recovered through administration fees feed into the annual superannuation performance test, which assesses administration fees against the median for the product category on a combined basis with investment performance, with two consecutive failures prohibiting new members.
audit_trail.basis: Chain: (1) the performance test benchmarks administration fees charged in the last financial year against a category median; (2) Division 296 costs recovered through those fees enter that metric; (3) because the benchmark is a median, a licensee with a small affected population relative to total membership spreads the same fixed build cost over a smaller base and moves against the median. The test mechanics are sourced from the legislated performance test framework but were not re-read this pass; the transmission mechanism and the resulting incentive to absorb rather than transparently recover the cost are APRA's own analysis.

audit_trail.assertion: Defined benefit earnings are measured as the movement in the actuarial value of the member's interest, adjusted for contributions and withdrawals and multiplied by a prescribed reduction factor of 0.825; the resulting liability is deferred to a debt account until the end benefit is paid, so there is no near-term call on fund solvency.
audit_trail.basis: Practitioner analysis of the draft regulations (Grant Thornton) for the 0.825 factor; ATO guidance on paying Division 296 tax for the deferral to a debt account. The factor was verified against the draft, not the made regulations.

audit_trail.assertion: The single unisex pensioner mortality basis using male rates is not a closed question.
audit_trail.basis: The Actuaries Institute's 7 April 2026 submission welcomes the single unisex male-rate basis; ASFA's submission of the same date contains a live section headed 'Use of only male valuation factors'. Two peak bodies were in disagreement at the close of consultation and the position adopted in the made regulations has not been confirmed, so the draft register's statement that the issue is closed has been withdrawn.

audit_trail.assertion: The realised-earnings base taxes distribution and disposal but not accrual, which is a deferral incentive whose system-level tendency is toward low-distribution, low-turnover, capital-growth assets - the same direction as the illiquid-allocation trend APRA has already identified as a system risk.
audit_trail.basis: Original analytical proposition written for this meeting, unquantified. It is offered as the reason the system-level file should not be closed on the flow question alone, paired with the SRS 553.0 out-of-cycle valuation series (first reporting period the December 2025 quarter) as a clean pre-commencement monitoring baseline. No source makes this argument and no behavioural magnitude is claimed.

audit_trail.assertion: Third-party concentration is the largest operational fact about this measure: the calculation, attribution, ATO lodgement and release-authority payment will be delivered by a small number of shared administrators, custodians and external tax agents, so a methodology defect or build failure is a common-mode event across many funds in the same annual window, and accountability for the 'fair and reasonable' judgement is non-delegable even where a vendor computes it.
audit_trail.basis: Chain: (1) fund administration is a CPS 230 default critical operation and is predominantly outsourced across the sector; (2) CPS 230's service provider limb applies and APRA already holds material service provider registers submitted by 1 October 2025 for concentration-risk purposes; (3) shared administrators mean shared methodology, which produces consistency within a bloc and a cliff between blocs, and means boards will in substance adopt a vendor's judgement; (4) the trustee remains accountable. The concentration pattern is inferred from the structure of the sector, not from the registers themselves, which have not been analysed for this purpose - doing so is the recommended first step and requires no new collection.

audit_trail.assertion: Small APRA funds are APRA-regulated, have six or fewer members, and therefore fall on the prescribed-formula-plus-annual-actuarial-certificate side of the regime rather than the trustee-judgement side that the rest of the analysis addresses.
audit_trail.basis: Chain: (1) the regime splits at six members, not at SMSF versus APRA-regulated; (2) small APRA funds are defined by having no more than six members and are trusteed by RSE licensees APRA supervises; (3) therefore a subset of APRA's own supervised population faces a different legal mechanism, including a recurring annual actuarial certificate cost that may be uneconomic for very small funds. The fund count (approximately 673 at June 2025) was not re-verified this pass.

audit_trail.assertion: The Council of Financial Regulators is not the right forum for an APRA-ATO coordination question, because the CFR has four members - APRA, ASIC, Treasury and the RBA - and the ATO is not one of them.
audit_trail.basis: CFR member agencies page (https://www.cfr.gov.au/about/member-agencies.html) - confirmed this pass. The note refers instead to the broader grouping that includes the ATO.

audit_trail.assertion: Whether the ATO can lawfully provide APRA with member-level or fund-level Division 296 and total-balance data is a threshold legal question governed by the taxation secrecy provisions in Schedule 1 Division 355 of the TAA 1953 and by APRA's own secrecy obligations, and it is unresolved.
audit_trail.basis: Chain: (1) the note recommends an ATO data exchange as the principal answer to APRA's visibility problem; (2) ATO disclosure of protected information is restricted by statute with defined exceptions; (3) therefore the recommendation may require an amendment or a legislated exception rather than an administrative arrangement, and the existing APRA-ATO memorandum of understanding may not cover it. The Division 355 provisions were not read this pass; the point is raised as a question to be resolved before the recommendation is put externally, not as a legal conclusion.

audit_trail.assertion: The recommendations in this note are options for consideration, and the grading rule is stated on the page and applied mechanically, with any judgement override declared in one line.
audit_trail.basis: Editorial and methodological decision for this meeting, made in response to review findings that the draft's grades were not monotonic in their own scores (two pairs of items with identical or dominating score vectors carried different grades) and that likelihood had been scored against whether a fact obtains rather than whether an adverse consequence crystallises in a named window. Likelihood is now stated as a dated proposition for each issue, and the A-grade count falls accordingly.

redteam_disposition.attack: FATAL. Consultation ask 8 quotes the ATO as being 'in the position of having retrospective law'. That statement is from June 2025 and is an artefact of the abandoned 1 July 2025 commencement; under the enacted law Assent (13 March 2026) precedes commencement (1 July 2026), so there is no retrospectivity.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Correct and independently checked against the enacted timeline. Quote deleted. The successor fund transfer protocol ask survives on its own footing and is re-grounded on transfers spanning the 30 June 2027 measurement date. Carrying a stale-design quote into a CEO-level note is exactly the failure mode this pass exists to catch.

redteam_disposition.attack: FATAL. Likelihood is scored against whether a fact is presently true rather than whether an adverse consequence occurs. All six likelihood-5 scores are present-tense certainties, which manufactures five of the six A grades.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: The criticism is methodologically decisive. Likelihood is redefined as P(named adverse consequence within a dated window) and every score restated as a dated proposition. Four of the six 5s fall to 2-3. A grades fall from six to three. No counter-argument available: a probability of 5 on a certainty is not a probability.

redteam_disposition.attack: FATAL. No stated rule maps materiality/likelihood/proximity to A/B/C, and the mapping is non-monotonic (P6 and P9 share a score vector but differ in grade; P15 dominates P14 but grades lower).
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Verified by adding the columns. Rule now stated on the page (A = proximity>=4 and materiality>=4 and likelihood>=4; B = otherwise sum>=10; C = sum<10) and applied mechanically, with any judgement override stated in one line. An unstated rubric is indefensible in front of a reader who can do arithmetic.

redteam_disposition.attack: FATAL. P6 grades a Division 296 outflow window as A while P16 finds this is not a liquidity event and instructs the note to open with that. The register contradicts itself on its own headline proposition.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Genuine internal contradiction; whichever the reader saw second would discredit the other. Resolved in favour of P16, which is the better-evidenced position. P6 is demoted and folded into the liquidity item as 'tested and cleared, with two named exceptions' (illiquid member-directed options; the June 2027 transitional window).

redteam_disposition.attack: FATAL. P14 recommends APRA tell licensees not to build to the post-death attribution rule because it is 'draft'. It is not draft: the regulations were made 11 June and registered 18 June 2026 with the rule intact.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: This was the only recommendation in the register capable of causing direct harm if adopted - telling supervised entities not to implement operative law. Instruction deleted and inverted: the rule is made, licensees must build to it, and the supervisory question is how continued post-death attribution is reconciled with the duty to cash death benefits as soon as practicable. Treasury advocacy on the merits is retained but moved to the consultation list.

redteam_disposition.attack: FATAL. P2 is graded A, labelled 'sourced', and rests on an unverified negative (APRA absent from the ATO working group / has published nothing), while ignoring bilateral Treasury-ATO-APRA engagement.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Independently confirmed: APRA does engage bilaterally with Treasury and the ATO, and the outstanding calculation/attribution work is progressing through an ATO co-design process. The 'no voice / not in the room' framing was wrong and is removed. The item is no longer a graded prudential risk; it becomes an ungraded APRA action - formalise participation in the Division 296 workstream so a prudential perspective is contributed before the ruling reaches draft - and is written as an opportunity, not a criticism of current practice.

redteam_disposition.attack: FATAL. CPS 230 is cited five times and only ever the critical-operations limb. The service provider limb (concentration in a handful of administrators, custodians and tax agents building one Division 296 engine for many funds) is never engaged, despite APRA already holding the material service provider register.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: The largest structural hole and it undercuts the note's own claim that the exposure is operational. A standalone issue is added covering common-mode failure across client funds in a single correlated annual window, non-delegable trustee accountability where a vendor forms the methodology in substance, the 'administrator cannot deliver' failure mode, and the point that the concentration map already exists in the MSP register at zero collection cost. The CPS 230 framework verdict is rewritten as a two-limb assessment.

redteam_disposition.attack: CPS 230 para 24 is misquoted throughout; the 'must manage its full range of operational risks' duty is para 24. Para 23 is senior management's duty to inform the Board.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Independently verified. Corrected in P1, P3, P8 and both framework verdicts. A repeated off-by-one on the register's most-cited standard would have been corrected in the room.

redteam_disposition.attack: SPS 530 para 31 is not the investment stress testing programme; para 31 is, confirmed by para 38's own cross-reference.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Independently verified. Citation changed to para 31 and the range restated as paras 31-38 throughout. Para 36(d)/(e) references are unaffected and retained.

redteam_disposition.attack: The elective 30 June 2026 cost-base reset is available to small funds - SMSFs and small APRA funds - not to SMSFs alone. The legislated boundary is fund size, not SMSF versus APRA-regulated, which weakens P7's perimeter framing.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Correct and consequential: small APRA funds sit inside APRA's own perimeter and on the favourable side of the line. P7 is restated around the size boundary, and the perimeter argument (migration to SMSFs) is separated from the design-asymmetry argument (large funds and pooled superannuation trusts disadvantaged against small funds, including APRA-regulated ones).

redteam_disposition.attack: Four load-bearing quotes attributed to 2026 ATO Superannuation Administration Group key messages are in fact from the 17 June 2025 meeting; a reader following the citations will not find them.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Provenance failure. All four re-cited to the 17 June 2025 meeting with its own URL and each flagged as predating the October 2025 redesign and the made regulations, so a reader can judge whether it has been overtaken. This also drove the fatal 'retrospective law' error.

redteam_disposition.attack: P13 recommends APRA push back on reuse of the Division 293 SuperStream codes, without disclosing that ASFA expressly asked the ATO to reuse that channel on cost grounds.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Briefing the Chair to advocate against the peak body's stated position without saying so is indefensible. ASFA's request is disclosed and the ask is reframed to a machine-readable Division 296 flag on the existing message plus a commitment that the flow can be isolated in fund and regulator reporting - which meets APRA's classification objective without the build cost ASFA is guarding.

redteam_disposition.attack: The $2,018bn and 18.7m accounts belong to the 23 licensees reviewed, not the 12 requiring material improvement. The register roughly doubles the apparent scale of the adverse finding.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Verified against APRA's own December 2024 publication. Restated so the review scope, the 12, and the eight-licensee liquidity subgroup (27% of funds under management, 5.4m accounts) are separately attributed. This is the number most likely to be repeated verbatim and then corrected.

redteam_disposition.attack: P5 builds a named supervisory shortlist on CSS at 23.58% of accounts above $1m while P10 disclaims the same entity's balance-bracket data as a probable reporting artefact.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: The register cannot rely on a figure in one issue and disclaim it in another. CSS is moved to 'subject to data verification' pending confirmation with Commonwealth Superannuation Corporation, and the CSS headline number is struck. The shortlist survives on the platform and wrap cohort, which does not depend on the disputed data.

redteam_disposition.attack: The ATO law companion ruling quote is cited to the advice-under-development page, which does not contain it - and the same page is simultaneously cited for the finding that no Division 296 item appears on it.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Both cannot be true of one page. The negative finding is retained against that URL; the drafting statement is either re-cited to its actual source or, if it cannot be located, dropped to a gap. No citation is retained on a page that does not carry the quoted words.

redteam_disposition.attack: P16's 'one fifteenth of a peak stress-test month' mixes numerators - it uses the APRA-side $0.9bn for the lump-sum comparison and the whole-system $2.3bn for the stress-test comparison; the unexplained 0.4-1.1% range has no stated basis.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Arithmetic checked and the criticism holds. One numerator is now used throughout ($0.9bn APRA-side): about 1.1% of annual lump sums, about 0.03% of assets, about 3% of a single peak stress-test month. The unexplained range is deleted. This is the sentence the note proposes to open with, so it must survive arithmetic.

redteam_disposition.attack: 'Met it without selling a single unlisted asset' is categorical; APRA's own wording is that funds largely avoided selling unlisted assets, meeting the shock primarily through listed equities.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: The source does not support the categorical claim and the sentence is load-bearing for the note's calibration. Replaced with APRA's own wording. The P6 quote is downgraded to a paraphrase pending verification against the full report.

redteam_disposition.attack: P1 and P12 overstate trustee finality: the attribution is an input to a Commissioner's assessment, and the member retains an objection right against the ATO regardless of any AFCA carve-out.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Correct, and it materially changes the remedy landscape. P1 is reframed - the trustee determines the input that drives the assessment. P12 now states that a carve-out removes the AFCA route but not the statutory objection route, and the ask becomes whether an objection against the ATO is a real remedy when the disputed judgement sits with a third party. Note this cuts both ways: the enacting law's express AFCA note on the provider's notification duty shows Parliament contemplated complaints against providers, which weakens the industry carve-out request.

redteam_disposition.attack: P10 declares the gender-equity concern 'closed' on the Actuaries Institute's endorsement while ASFA was still making submissions on male-only valuation factors at the close of consultation.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Declaring an issue closed to a CEO on one body's endorsement while another's contemporaneous submission is open is an assurance the note cannot give. Downgraded to a statement of both positions, with the made-regulation position to be confirmed before treating it as settled.

redteam_disposition.attack: P6 and P9 have identical score vectors (3/4/5) but different grades.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Resolved by the stated rubric plus the demotion of P6 required by the liquidity contradiction. Under the rule both sit at B; P6 is then folded into the liquidity item and P9 retains its own entry.

redteam_disposition.attack: P15 strictly dominates P14 on the declared scores yet is graded one band lower.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: A second independent inversion. Fixed by the stated rubric and by the separate uplift to P15's proximity, which places it above P14 on both score and grade.

redteam_disposition.attack: The RFI timing (10 business days from November 2027; 28 calendar days from April 2028) is cited jointly to two ATO meetings that say different things, and the non-defined-benefit date appears to have moved from February to April.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: The two sources are not consistent and the register presented them as if they were. Each meeting is now cited separately, the schedule change is disclosed, the years are marked as ATO indicative planning dates rather than settled, and the tension with 'assessments issue in the second half of 2027-28' is stated as an open question rather than smoothed over.

redteam_disposition.attack: P6's grade A ignores the size of the liability: a member at $3.2m pays about $1,800 and cannot rationally restructure for that, while a member at $8-10m has a real liability but cannot get under $3m by 30 June 2027. Both tails argue against a correlated rush.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: The arithmetic is correct (proportioning by (TSB-3m)/TSB then 15%) and it is the strongest single piece of analysis in the red-team pack. Likelihood cut, P6 demoted to C, and the $1,800 / $9,000 / $63,000 figures moved to the front of the note as the register's missing denominator. The supervisory action - requiring production of the policy-driven liquidity scenario - is retained as a cheap test.

redteam_disposition.attack: P1's materiality 5 is the register's only 5 and nothing measures it; the spread between two lawful attribution methods is never estimated.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Accepted that an unmeasured 5 cannot stand: materiality drops to 4 pending evidence, and the proposed test (ask two or three exposed licensees to run two defensible methods over FY2026-27 data to date and report the spread) is adopted as a pre-meeting action. Not fully accepted: the reviewer's premise that every lawful method 'must be broadly proportionate to member balances' is itself unsourced - the statute says only 'fair and reasonable' - so the inference that dispersion is structurally small is not established either. The score moves because the evidence is absent, not because the reviewer's alternative is proved.

redteam_disposition.attack: The register cites 305,000 accounts above $1m averaging $1.45m to argue APRA is blind, and never turns the same data round to bound the in-scope population, so no issue has a denominator.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Correct and cheap to fix. A labelled inference is added: a steeply decaying right tail above $1m, read against Treasury's superseded-design estimate of 31,800 in-scope individuals across all APRA-regulated and exempt public sector funds, implies a median large licensee has in-scope members in the hundreds. Marked 'inferred', with the Treasury vintage caveat carried, and used to calibrate supervisory intensity and the proportionality gate in the readiness item.

redteam_disposition.attack: P9 (valuation still determines the tax) is undergraded at B; it is the one issue where APRA has already published adverse findings on the precise control that now carries a personal tax consequence, and the sharper risk is upward revaluation pushing members over the threshold.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: The substantive insight is accepted and incorporated: upward revaluation at 30 June is the more likely complaints channel, since downward suppression requires alleging misconduct and harms every other member's exit price. The regrade to A is not accepted - under the now-stated rubric a 3/4/5 vector is B, and creating an unexplained override for this item would reintroduce the very inconsistency the rubric was adopted to cure. P9 is the highest-ranked B and is flagged as such, with the reputational point made in the text rather than through the grade.

redteam_disposition.attack: P15 (the total superannuation balance redefinition) is undergraded at C on proximity 2; the trustee reports the number and members will act on it, and the failure mode - an excess contributions assessment from a methodology-driven balance movement - is concrete and member-harming.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Accepted. Proximity raised and the issue regraded to B, with the excess-contributions failure mode stated. The population is far larger than the Division 296 cohort and the trustee sits at the centre of the disclosure. The unexplained '$1.5 million' figure quoted from ASFA is flagged as unverified rather than repeated.

redteam_disposition.attack: P3's likelihood 5 measures commencement rather than risk, and its statement that absence from the risk appetite statement, risk declaration, operational risk financial requirement target or business plan is 'a governance finding' has no materiality gate.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Both limbs accepted. Likelihood rescored against a failed or materially wrong first RFI response in the 2028 window. The governance-finding statement is gated on exposure, using the in-scope headcount inference above, so a licensee with a handful of affected members is not held to the same expectation as a licensee with thousands. An ungated expectation would not survive contact with a small licensee.

redteam_disposition.attack: P3, P13 and P8 are one operational-risk theme (fund administration performing a new statutory calculation and payment function on external clocks) split into three graded entries, inflating the apparent breadth of the register.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: They share instruments but not duties, clocks, failure modes or remedies. P3 is a build-and-respond capability question on an annual RFI window; P13 is an externally triggered payment obligation out of preserved benefits; P8 is a multi-year records and reproducibility obligation now reinforced by an independent statutory duty on the provider to notify the Commissioner within 14 days of an end benefit becoming payable and to correct a material error within 7 days - a duty that has nothing to do with release-authority payment and would be buried by a merge. The grade-inflation concern is real but is cured by the stated rubric and the rescoring, which is the proportionate remedy; collapsing three distinct obligations to fix a scoring artefact would lose the one genuinely new duty the enacting law imposes on funds.

redteam_disposition.attack: P5 bootstraps: findings on unlisted valuation and liquidity frameworks, and enforcement on investment governance, are treated as evidence of unreadiness for a tax calculation performed by different systems and teams.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: The inference does not hold and would be spotted immediately. The reasoning is replaced with the sound one the reviewer supplies: platform and wrap trustees are the right cohort because member-directed options make attribution genuinely hard and genuinely divergent. The December 2024 thematic is retained only as indicative evidence of general governance capacity, expressly flagged as indicative rather than probative.

redteam_disposition.attack: P7's title asserts money is already moving while the body concedes causation is not established, and the largest rollover quarter predates the October 2025 redesign.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Accepted that the title over-claims: retitled around the legislated cost-base asymmetry, with the rollover series demoted to a monitoring line and materiality reduced. Not accepted in its reasoning: the September 2025 quarter predates the redesign but not the measure, which had been public policy since February 2023, so that quarter does not refute a Division 296 explanation any more than it supports one. The correct position is that causation is unestablished in both directions and APRA should say so plainly.

redteam_disposition.attack: P8's materiality 4 is defeated by its own evidence: ASFA puts typical amendment variation at a few basis points, so per-member tax changes are trivial. The real point is administrative disproportion and four-year reproducibility.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Accepted that member financial harm is not the right frame and that materiality must come down; the issue is reframed around reissuing assessments to move a bill by tens of dollars, which is the strongest argument for the industry's materiality-threshold ask. Not demoted as far as C: the four-year reproducibility obligation now sits alongside an express statutory correction duty on the provider within 7 days of a material change or omission, which is a live, dated compliance obligation rather than a hypothetical, so the issue holds at B.

redteam_disposition.attack: P13 states the ten-business-day release authority clock and penalty as settled fact in plain English while its own gap records that the Division 296 release authority type is unconfirmed.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: An unconfirmed statutory deadline cannot sit in the plain-English text with the caveat three fields away. Rewritten to state that other release authority types carry a ten-business-day clock and a penalty and that the Division 296 equivalent has not been published, pending confirmation with the ATO before the meeting.

redteam_disposition.attack: P12 overstates APRA's proximity (AFCA jurisdiction is ASIC and Treasury territory) and recommends an ATO data request that taxpayer confidentiality does not permit.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: The secrecy point is accepted in full: the ask is reframed as a legislative request to Treasury for a disclosure exception, with the obstacle stated. The AFCA point is accepted only in part - the question is routed to ASIC with an APRA member-outcomes view attached rather than owned by APRA - but the proximity downgrade is rejected, because the enacting law's own notification provision carries an express note that a dissatisfied person may complain under the AFCA scheme. Parliament has therefore already contemplated member complaints against providers arising from Division 296 conduct, which is squarely a supervised-entity conduct and operational exposure.

redteam_disposition.attack: P10 frames the accumulation/defined benefit differential tax base as an equitable-treatment failing, but a trustee cannot breach the covenant by complying with a statute that prescribes different bases.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Category error accepted. The equity framing is demoted to a member-communications point and the issue leads on what is genuinely trustee-side: the new annual actuarial valuation capability, the tighter response window, and decades-long deferred debt account tracking that must survive mergers and administrator changes. The 10,000 defined benefit members figure is caveated to the same standard as the other superseded-design numbers.

redteam_disposition.attack: P11's materiality 3 is unsupported: roughly $1.42m sector-wide (or even ten times that) spread across 22.5m accounts is cents per member, which is a governance-of-process point, not a member-outcomes harm.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: The arithmetic is right and belongs in the note. Materiality reduced and the issue regraded, while the recommended action is kept unchanged - asking how build and run costs are recovered before FY2028 fee-setting is locked in is cheap, timely and useful, and the cohort proposal for business performance reviews is among the best instrument-level ideas in the pack. A lower-grade issue with a strong action is recorded as such.

redteam_disposition.attack: About half the consultation asks are tax-design positions advanced in APRA's name (cost-base levelling, materiality thresholds, reserve treatment, post-death attribution, loss treatment, pooled superannuation trust mechanics) rather than prudential consequences.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Accepted in structure: the list is split into asks APRA owns (participation in the calculation and attribution work, the transfer protocol, a published in-scope headcount, an ATO data arrangement, and a minimum governance standard for attribution as a member-equity expectation) and prudential consequences put on the record for Treasury and the ATO to remedy. Not accepted that the substance should be dropped - a prudential regulator is entitled, and expected, to state the consequence for supervised entities and members of a specific design feature; what it should not do is nominate the tax mechanic. Each relocated item is restated as a consequence with the remedy left to the policy owner.

redteam_disposition.attack: P15's plain English fails: 'superannuation interest' is an undefined term of art and is the crux of the issue.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Rewritten in the reviewer's terms - each separate pot of super gets its own value, the total decides whether more money can be put in, and for defined benefit members the number can move because the measuring method changed rather than because their money changed. The note is unreadable at CEO level if the crux is a term of art.

redteam_disposition.attack: P10's plain English packs actuarial value, the movement measure and the 0.825 factor into one clause and assumes the reader knows what a family law split valuation is.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Rewritten to explain that an actuary must estimate what a promised pension is worth, that the tax looks at how much that estimate rose over the year cut by about 17.5%, and that funds have only ever done this one member at a time, by hand, on divorce. Without that, a reader cannot judge whether the capability build is proportionate.

redteam_disposition.attack: No issue anywhere states what an affected member actually pays, so the proportioning mechanism - only the share of earnings above the threshold is taxed - is never explained and every materiality judgement is untestable.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: The single most useful omission identified. A worked example is added at the front of the note ($3.2m about $1,800; $4m about $9,000; $10m about $63,000, with the arithmetic shown and labelled as APRA's own derivation), and every likelihood and materiality score is re-tested against it. This alone drove the demotion of the outflow issue.

redteam_disposition.attack: P2 recommends escalating an APRA-ATO coordination gap to the Council of Financial Regulators, of which the ATO is not a member; the relevant forum is the wider CFR Plus grouping. The register also recommends an ATO data exchange three times without checking whether taxation secrecy permits it.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Both accepted. The forum is corrected, and the legal-basis question - whether the taxation secrecy provisions and the existing APRA-ATO arrangements permit member-level or fund-level Division 296 data to be shared, or whether a legislated exception is needed - is added as the threshold step before any data-exchange recommendation. Recommending a data flow without establishing that it is lawful is a hole a Treasury or ATO counterpart would find immediately.

redteam_disposition.attack: The register misses APRA's own Payday Super readiness letter of 25 March 2026 - a four-month-old, self-authored precedent for exactly the intervention the register proposes, on a measure commencing the same day.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Strongest completeness addition. It supplies a precedent, drafting, and an answer to the 'is this APRA's business?' objection, and it makes the proposed Division 296 letter a consistency step rather than a new initiative. Cited in the engagement and readiness items. The related change-saturation point - both measures first applying from 1 July 2026 on the same platforms and the same finite administrator change capacity - is added as a distinct operational risk.

redteam_disposition.attack: P11 stops at fee-setting governance and misses the transmission mechanism: costs recovered through administration fees feed the annual performance test, which carries a product-closure consequence. Regrade to A.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: The transmission mechanism is accepted and added, together with the perverse incentive it creates to absorb or capitalise the cost rather than recover it transparently. The regrade to A is rejected: the performance test benchmarks administration fees against the median for the product category, so a cost incurred by the whole sector moves the median as well as the licensee, and the effect is differential rather than absolute. It bites only where a licensee's affected population is small relative to its fee base - a real but narrow exposure, better stated as a supervisory question than as a top-tier risk. The performance test citation is also marked for verification before it is put in front of the CEO.

redteam_disposition.attack: P10 cites SPS 231 Outsourcing, which was replaced by CPS 230 on 1 July 2025, so the defined benefit actuarial capability question is analysed under a repealed standard.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Verified and corrected to the CPS 230 service provider provisions. The substitution also improves the analysis: a small number of consulting actuarial firms will perform the new annual valuation for essentially every defined benefit scheme in the country on a short response clock, which is a service provider concentration exposure in its own right and now sits with the broader concentration issue.

redteam_disposition.attack: The register identifies that RSE auditor assurance does not reach the Division 296 calculation but never runs the same reasoning on breach reporting: Division 296 obligations arise under tax law, not RSE licensee law, so a failed ATO report is not of itself notifiable to APRA.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: The reasoning is sound and yields three layered blind spots - no APRA reporting standard, no auditor assurance, no notification trigger - of which the register found one. Added, with the fix that costs nothing: state in the proposed letter that APRA expects notification of material Division 296 failures, mirroring the Payday Super approach. Noted alongside it that the enacting law does impose a direct notification duty on the provider, but to the Commissioner and not to APRA, which sharpens rather than weakens the point.

redteam_disposition.attack: The perimeter analysis has only one channel. Members can also reduce their measured balance via life-company lifetime income streams, and money leaving super often goes to investment bonds - both APRA-regulated products, so part of the supposed perimeter loss is a transfer within APRA's own perimeter.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Accepted as a monitoring item, labelled inferred and unquantified. It usefully reframes the CEO conversation from loss of visibility to an internal coordination step with life insurance supervision that costs nothing, and it connects to the total superannuation balance valuation changes already identified elsewhere in the register.

redteam_disposition.attack: The liquidity item closes the system-level file after testing only aggregate outflow. A realised-earnings base is a deferral incentive that tilts portfolios toward low-distribution, low-turnover illiquid assets - compounding a trend APRA has already flagged.
redteam_disposition.reasoning: Not carried into the note. In pooled options asset allocation is set for the whole option and a trustee cannot tilt it to suit fewer than 0.5% of members without running straight into the equitable-treatment covenant, so the proposed mechanism has no route to operate at scale. Where it does operate directly - member-directed and platform options - the effect is already captured by the platform and attribution issues. What remains is an unquantified, unsourced macro-allocation claim in a domain owned by Treasury and the RBA; advancing it as an original APRA proposition in a CEO-level note invites a challenge the note cannot answer, which is precisely the risk this pass is meant to remove. Recorded here as a considered rejection rather than an oversight, and noted as a question APRA could pose internally if it wishes to test it with evidence.

residual_uncertainties: The ATO's law companion ruling on calculating Division 296 fund earnings and members' relevant super earnings is still unwritten and unpublished. As at the page's 6 July 2026 update, no Division 296 item appears on the ATO's advice-under-development programme, which lists five unrelated items. Until it issues, no authoritative statement exists of how the calculation is to be performed, and the ruling's move from draft to final is the point at which the method effectively fixes.

The operative attribution text in F2026L00726 could not be read directly - the Federal Register serves instrument documents through a JavaScript front end. The 'more than six members' boundary, the 'fair and reasonable' wording, the prescribed formula and actuarial certificate for small funds, and the prescribed defined benefit reduction factor of 0.825 all rest on the Bills Digest, industry submissions and practitioner commentary on the draft, not on the made instrument. The register's earlier phase-in factors (20/40/60/80 per cent) were drawn from two practitioner readings of the draft and are not carried in the note.

Consequently it is not confirmed whether the made regulations adopted any of the following, each of which industry requested and each of which changes a recommendation in the note: a materiality threshold (5 per cent was proposed by two bodies) and an extended reporting window on amended fund tax returns; a fix for pooled superannuation trusts with multiple options or unitholders; a prescribed treatment of unallocated reserves; a bulk 30 June 2026 cost-base declaration for member-directed options in large funds; and the treatment of losses, specifically whether member-level earnings are floored at nil with no carry-forward and whether a loss in one interest can offset a gain in another.
