The ATO's information-request timetable is internally inconsistent across its own published records. The 18 February 2026 Superannuation Administration Group key messages record defined benefit requests from November 2027 and other APRA-fund requests from February 2028; the 20 May 2026 key messages say November and April with no year stated. Neither reconciles cleanly with assessments issuing in the second half of 2027-28. The dates should be treated as indicative ATO planning that has already moved once, and confirmed before any supervisory timetable is built on them.

Whether AFCA jurisdiction over a trustee's 'fair and reasonable' attribution will be curtailed is unresolved and points in two directions. s 134-140 of Schedule 1 to the TAA 1953 carries an express note contemplating AFCA complaints about provider conduct under this regime; ASFA asked Treasury to place attribution judgements outside AFCA review. It is separately doubtful that income tax regulations could curtail AFCA at all, since its jurisdiction derives from the Corporations Act scheme approval and the AFCA Rules, which is ASIC and Treasury territory rather than APRA's. The member's statutory right to object to the ATO assessment persists either way, but whether that is a real remedy when the disputed judgement was made by a third party is untested.

The dispersion between two lawful 'fair and reasonable' attribution methods applied to the same fund and the same members has never been measured, and nothing in the public record estimates it. This is the single most consequential unknown in the note: if the spread is a few basis points of attributed earnings, the attribution issue is a platform and member-directed-option problem rather than an industry-wide one; if it is percentage points, it is the central issue. The recommended test - asking two or three exposed licensees to run two defensible methods over their year-to-date data and report the spread - would resolve it before the first measurement year closes.

No current in-scope headcount exists under the enacted design, at sector level or per licensee. The only Commonwealth figure - 31,800 of approximately 80,000 individuals - is from the January 2024 Impact Analysis, struck on 2022-vintage data under the superseded change-in-balance design, and it combines APRA-regulated funds with exempt public sector schemes that APRA does not supervise. Without a denominator, supervisory intensity cannot be calibrated and a licensee claiming minimal exposure cannot be challenged.

The integrity of APRA's fund-level balance-bracket data for the largest Commonwealth defined benefit schemes is in doubt. PSS and MilitarySuper report fewer than 20 accounts above $1m against average balances near $585,000 and $546,000, with most accounts clustered in a single bracket. CSS, reported by the same entity on the same form, is the largest single concentration in the exposed-cohort analysis. Until Commonwealth Superannuation Corporation confirms the reporting, CSS should not be used as a headline figure.

Causation of the growth in net rollovers to SMSFs is not established and probably cannot be from published data. The largest single quarter precedes the redesign announcement, and the best establishment data attributes growth to different drivers and a younger demographic. The legislated cost-base asymmetry is real; the flow series does not evidence its effect.

Whether the male-only unisex mortality basis was settled in the made regulations is unknown. Two peak bodies were in disagreement at the close of consultation - the Actuaries Institute welcoming it, ASFA still submitting on it - and the draft register's statement that the question is closed has been withdrawn.

The final form of post-death attribution is not confirmed against the made instrument. Practitioner commentary on release indicates the draft approach survived and a 'death benefit income stream' concept was added, but sources conflict on whether a deceased member's total superannuation balance is set to nil so no further liability accrues, or whether attribution continues to the undistributed interest until death benefits are fully paid. The two readings produce materially different trustee obligations.

Whether Division 296 release authorities carry the ten-business-day payment clock and the 20-penalty-unit non-compliance exposure has not been published. The ATO's list of release authority types for APRA-regulated funds shows six categories and does not include Division 296. The specific condition-of-release item authorising release of preserved benefits for this purpose was also not identified.

The legal gateway for any ATO-to-APRA data exchange is unresolved: whether the taxation secrecy provisions in Schedule 1 Division 355 of the TAA 1953 permit disclosure of total-balance or Division 296 outflow data to APRA, whether the existing APRA-ATO memorandum of understanding covers it, and whether a legislated exception is required. The note's principal answer to its own principal visibility problem may not be administratively available.

The trust-law layer beneath the operational analysis is untested. Whether an RSE's governing rules permit debiting a member's interest to satisfy a Division 296 release authority, and whether they permit recovering build and run costs from members, has not been checked and may require deed amendments across the industry before the first release authorities arrive.

Where a trustee's attribution error causes a member a personal tax detriment or a penalty, it is unknown whether the trustee may indemnify itself from fund assets consistently with the SIS Act restrictions on indemnity, and whether the operational risk financial requirement - which is members' money - may lawfully be applied to compensate an individual's personal tax liability. Either answer has a significant member-equity consequence and neither has been researched.

Two reporting-side questions remain open: whether SRS 710.0 Conditions of Release or SRS 610.1 Changes in Membership Profile already decompose outflows by reason, which would partly close the flow-visibility gap; and whether confidentiality and re-identification constraints would prevent publication of fund-level counts in a $10m+ balance bracket, which bears on the claim that adding brackets to SRS 611.0 is a cheap change.

It is not known whether the remediation plans arising from APRA's December 2024 valuation and liquidity thematic have been delivered and closed out. The exposed-cohort recommendation assumes they have not, and should be checked internally before the meeting.

The extent and form of APRA's engagement with Treasury and the ATO on this measure since October 2025 is known to exist but not documented in this work. The finding that APRA has published nothing Division 296-specific is search-based and should be confirmed against APRA's own publication records before being stated externally.

Whether the s 29JA breach-notification analysis is legally correct has not been confirmed against the provision's text. If a Division 296 failure is in fact notifiable on some other basis, the recommended letter is unnecessary; if it is not, the letter is the cheapest available fix.

Several populations named in the note remain unanalysed for want of time: exempt public sector schemes and unfunded state schemes, which are outside APRA's supervision but inside the Commonwealth's affected-population estimate; constitutionally protected funds; crediting-rate and smoothed-return funds, where the note's unit-pricing governance analogy does not reach; deferred and innovative income streams; and migration into life-company lifetime income streams and investment bonds, which would move members between two parts of APRA's own perimeter rather than out of it. Each is identified as a gap rather than asserted.
